choices: DATE_TRUNC the timestamp to month, GROUP BY the truncated month — time-series analysis needs a consistent time grain before aggregating
GROUP BY the raw timestamp — each second is a group
Time grain doesn't matter for trends
Use string formatting for months
evidence: q.sql
scenarios.hint: What does one row of the result represent — a second, or a month?
scenarios.prompt: How do you build a monthly trend?
scenarios.situation: 'Signups per month' — a junior analyst groups by the raw timestamp and gets millions of groups.
scenarios.title: The timestamp groups
scenarios.why: Time-series analysis starts by choosing the grain: DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) buckets timestamps to month starts, then GROUP BY aggregates. Without truncation, every distinct timestamp is its own group — noise, not trend. (Syntax varies: DATE_TRUNC in Postgres, DATETRUNC in T-SQL, DATE_FORMAT in MySQL — the concept is universal.) Also mind time zones: truncate in the business's time zone, not UTC, or month boundaries shift.

choices: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) — unique users; COUNT(*) counts events; the ratio is events per user — know which the question asks
COUNT(*) — it counts users
They are the same when grouped
COUNT(user_id) counts unique users
evidence: q.sql

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', ts) AS day,
 COUNT(*) AS events,
 COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users
FROM clicks GROUP BY 1;
scenarios.hint: If one user clicks 50 times, how many 'users' is that — and how many 'events'?
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference, and why does it matter?
scenarios.situation: 'Daily active users' computed with COUNT(*) shows 10x the known user base — power users dominate.
scenarios.title: The active-user inflation
scenarios.why: COUNT(*) counts rows (events); COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts unique users. 'Active users' = distinct users; 'engagement' might = events. Mixing them up inflates DAU by the activity of power users. The events-per-user ratio (COUNT(*)/COUNT(DISTINCT)) is itself a useful metric — but only when you know which numerator and denominator you're using.

choices: Cohort retention: GROUP BY signup month (cohort), then compute % active in each subsequent month — retention curves reveal whether the product keeps users
Overall monthly actives — it shows retention
Cohort analysis needs no SQL
Retention equals 1 minus churn always
evidence: q.sql

WITH cohorts AS (
 SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_at) AS cohort FROM users)
SELECT c.cohort,
 DATE_TRUNC('month', a.active_at) AS m,
 COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active
FROM cohorts c JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = c.user_id
GROUP BY 1, 2;
scenarios.hint: 'Users who signed up in January, what % were active in March?' — what two groupings do you need?
scenarios.prompt: How do you measure whether the product retains users?
scenarios.situation: Total signups grow, but nobody knows if users stick around. Overall actives look flat.
scenarios.title: The leaky bucket
scenarios.why: Cohort retention: group users by signup period (the cohort), then track each cohort's activity over subsequent periods — producing retention curves. Flat overall actives + growing signups = churn masking growth (the leaky bucket). Cohort curves show whether newer cohorts retain better (product improving) or all cohorts decay the same (structural problem). It's the core product-health analysis.

choices: Funnel with step-by-step conversion: count users reaching each stage (ordered), compute conversion between consecutive steps — drop-off pinpoints friction
Total conversions only — funnels add nothing
Funnel steps can be in any order
Conversion rates need no denominators
evidence: q.sql

WITH steps AS (
 SELECT user_id,
  MAX(CASE WHEN event='view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS viewed,
  MAX(CASE WHEN event='cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted,
  MAX(CASE WHEN event='buy' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS bought
 FROM events GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS users,
 SUM(viewed) AS viewed, SUM(carted) AS carted, SUM(bought) AS bought
FROM steps;
scenarios.hint: To find where users drop off, what do you need at each stage — and in what order?
scenarios.prompt: How do you build a conversion funnel in SQL?
scenarios.situation: 'Where do shoppers drop off?' — the team has event data but no funnel.
scenarios.title: The leaky funnel
scenarios.why: Funnel = ordered stages with per-stage user counts; conversion = stage_n / stage_{n-1}. The conditional-aggregation pattern (MAX(CASE WHEN event=...) per user) builds the funnel in one pass. The biggest drop-off between consecutive steps is where friction lives. Caveats: enforce event ordering (cart before buy), define the time window (session? 7 days?), and segment (mobile vs desktop funnels differ wildly).

choices: Window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1 — latest row per user without collapsing; or DISTINCT ON / QUALIFY per dialect
GROUP BY user_id with MAX(ts) — then join back for the full row
ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1 — gives one user's latest
Latest row per user is impossible in SQL
evidence: q.sql
scenarios.hint: Which pattern keeps the full row of each user's latest event?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get each user's current subscription status?
scenarios.situation: A subscriptions table has history rows per user. 'Current status per user' needs the latest row each.
scenarios.title: The current status
scenarios.why: ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by user ordered by time desc, filter rn=1 — the standard 'latest per group' pattern, returning full rows. (GROUP BY + MAX gets the timestamp but needs a self-join for the rest of the row.) Dialect shortcuts exist (Postgres DISTINCT ON, Snowflake/BigQuery QUALIFY). Every analyst needs this pattern — slowly-changing entity state is everywhere.

choices: Percent of total: SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () — window over the grouped result; or ratio-to-report patterns per dialect
Subquery computing the grand total, joined back — the only way
Percentages can't be computed in SQL
Divide by COUNT(*) instead
evidence: q.sql
scenarios.hint: After GROUP BY, what does SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () compute?
scenarios.prompt: How do you compute each region's share of total?
scenarios.situation: 'Each region's % of total sales' — the analyst writes two queries and divides in a spreadsheet.
scenarios.title: The share of total
scenarios.why: Window functions evaluate after GROUP BY: SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () = grand total over the grouped rows, so each row's share = its sum / grand total. One query, no spreadsheet round-trip. (Some dialects need a subquery/CTE: compute grouped sums, then window over them.) It's the 'percent of total' and 'running share' foundation.

scenarios.title: The Join That Multiplied Revenue
scenarios.situation: Your revenue-by-campaign report shows $4.2M, but finance's number is $1.1M. Your query joins orders to campaign_touchpoints on customer_id, and a customer can have multiple touchpoints. The query ran clean with no errors.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the correct fix?
choices: The join condition is wrong; join on order_id instead of customer_id
Use SELECT DISTINCT to remove the duplicates

It's a fan-out: each order row duplicates once per touchpoint, multiplying the summed revenue. Fix by aggregating orders to one row per customer (or per order) BEFORE joining, or join on the grain that matches the metric
The finance number is wrong; trust the query since it ran without errors
scenarios.why: Joining at mismatched grains fans out rows: one $100 order with 4 touchpoints becomes four $100 rows, and SUM counts it four times. DISTINCT doesn't fix it (rows differ by touchpoint columns). The rule: aggregate each side to the join grain before joining, or compute the metric at the correct grain first. 'No errors' never means 'correct' in SQL.
scenarios.hint: What happens to one order row when the customer it belongs to has four touchpoint rows?
evidence: Explain why SELECT DISTINCT does not fix a fan-out

scenarios.title: The Disappearing Nulls
scenarios.situation: You're computing average deal size by sales rep. One rep shows an average of $50K across 4 deals, but the CRM shows they actually closed 6 deals — two are stuck in 'negotiation' with NULL amounts. Your query uses AVG(amount) with no filter.
scenarios.prompt: How should you handle the NULLs, and what do you tell the stakeholder?
choices: AVG ignores NULLs automatically, so the $50K is correct as-is
Replace NULLs with the rep's average so the count stays at 6
Delete the NULL rows from the table to keep the data clean

Decide the business meaning first: if the question is 'average closed deal size', exclude NULLs explicitly and label it; if it's 'expected value per deal worked', COALESCE to 0 or model probability — then report the denominator (4 of 6) alongside the average so the stakeholder sees what's excluded
scenarios.why: AVG silently drops NULLs, so 'no filter' is actually an implicit business decision the stakeholder didn't make. The analyst's job is to surface the choice: closed-deal average vs pipeline-expected value are different questions with different NULL treatments. Reporting 'n=4 of 6 deals' makes the exclusion visible and auditable. Imputing the mean fabricates data; deleting rows destroys it.
scenarios.hint: AVG already made a decision about your NULLs — did anyone ask it to?
objectives: Make NULL-handling an explicit, labeled business decision
evidence: State two valid NULL treatments and the business question each answers

choices: Pivot table — drag-and-drop grouping/summarizing for exploration; formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS) for fixed, auditable calculations
Formulas for everything — pivots aren't reproducible
Pivot tables can't handle large data
VLOOKUP for aggregation
scenarios.hint: Exploring 'sales by region by quarter' interactively — formulas or drag-and-drop?
scenarios.prompt: When do you reach for a pivot table vs formulas?
scenarios.situation: An analyst writes 40 SUMIFS formulas to slice sales by region × quarter. The VP asks for 'by product too' — 40 more formulas.
scenarios.title: The formula sprawl
scenarios.why: Pivot tables are the exploration tool: drag fields to rows/columns/values, slice interactively, no formula maintenance. Formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS/XLOOKUP) suit fixed, repeatable calculations that must be auditable cell-by-cell. Rule: exploring → pivot; productionizing a fixed report → formulas (or better, SQL). 40 SUMIFS is a pivot table crying for help.

choices: XLOOKUP (or INDEX+MATCH) — looks left or right, exact match by default, handles missing gracefully; VLOOKUP only looks right and breaks when columns move
VLOOKUP — the standard; limitations are fine
VLOOKUP can look left with a flag
Lookup direction doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: The lookup column is to the RIGHT of the return column — which function handles that?
scenarios.prompt: Why has XLOOKUP replaced VLOOKUP?
scenarios.situation: A VLOOKUP breaks every time someone inserts a column; another needs to look left of the key column.
scenarios.title: The broken VLOOKUP
scenarios.why: VLOOKUP: searches the first column, returns from a column index to the right — brittle (column inserts shift the index) and one-directional. XLOOKUP (or INDEX+MATCH): separate lookup and return arrays — looks any direction, exact match default, built-in if-not-found handling. For analysts still on VLOOKUP: the upgrade removes an entire bug class.

choices: Clean first: TRIM whitespace, standardize case, fix date formats, split/merge columns, remove duplicates — analysis on dirty data is fiction
Analyze first; cleaning is optional
Dirty data averages out
Whitespace doesn't affect matching
scenarios.hint: 'New York' vs 'new york ' vs 'NEW YORK' — how many distinct values does the pivot see?
scenarios.prompt: What is the cleaning checklist before analysis?
scenarios.situation: A pivot shows 3 versions of 'New York'; dates mix US/EU formats; duplicates inflate counts.
scenarios.title: The dirty column
scenarios.why: Cleaning checklist: TRIM whitespace, UPPER/LOWER standardization, consistent date parsing (TEXTSPLIT or DATEVALUE with known format), dedupe (Remove Duplicates on key columns), handle blanks vs zeros explicitly. 'New York' × 3 = 3 groups in the pivot. Garbage in, gospel out is the analyst's original sin — clean before you conclude.

choices: One row per observation, one column per variable (tidy data); headers in row 1, no merged cells, no totals rows mixed into data — structure for analysis, format for presentation separately
Merged headers look professional — keep them
Totals rows inside the data are fine
Multiple tables per sheet is tidiest
scenarios.hint: Can a pivot table read a sheet with merged headers and subtotal rows mixed in?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a spreadsheet analysis-ready?
scenarios.situation: A 'report' sheet with merged headers, subtotal rows, and notes in cells can't be pivoted or imported.
scenarios.title: The unpivotable sheet
scenarios.why: Tidy structure: row 1 = single-row headers, one observation per row, one variable per column, no merged cells, no embedded totals/notes. Presentation formatting (merges, subtotals) belongs on a separate presentation sheet fed by formulas — never mixed into the data. If a pivot can't read it, it's not data, it's a picture of data.

choices: Spreadsheets are for exploration and small, manual work — beyond ~1M rows, multi-source joins, or scheduled refreshes, move to SQL/BI; version control is the hard limit
Spreadsheets scale infinitely
Version control works fine with emailed files
1M rows is plenty for any analysis
scenarios.hint: The file is emailed as 'final_v7_REALLY_FINAL.xlsx' — what broke?
scenarios.prompt: When do you outgrow spreadsheets?
scenarios.situation: A 2M-row 'analysis' spreadsheet crashes; three versions circulate by email; nobody can reproduce last month's numbers.
scenarios.title: The final_v7 spreadsheet
scenarios.why: Spreadsheet limits: row caps (~1M), no real version control (email chains), manual steps that don't reproduce, silent formula errors at scale. Graduate to SQL (data size, joins), BI tools (scheduled refresh, governed metrics), and version-controlled code when: data exceeds comfortable size, the analysis repeats on a schedule, or more than one person must reproduce it. Spreadsheets are the sketchpad, not the system.

choices: Data validation rules + conditional formatting for outliers + protected ranges — prevent bad input, highlight anomalies, lock formulas
More training for data enterers
Validation is unnecessary for internal sheets
Conditional formatting is decoration
scenarios.hint: A typo'd date breaks the monthly rollup — where should that typo have been caught?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make a shared input sheet trustworthy?
scenarios.situation: A team expense tracker: typos in dates and categories break the summary; someone overwrote a formula.
scenarios.title: The shared tracker
scenarios.why: Prevent, don't fix: data validation dropdowns constrain categories, date validation constrains formats, conditional formatting flags outliers/duplicates visually, and sheet protection locks formula cells while leaving inputs editable. A shared sheet without validation is a data-quality incident waiting for a deadline.

scenarios.title: The VLOOKUP That Lied
scenarios.situation: Your pricing sheet uses VLOOKUP to pull costs from a supplier table. After the supplier added new rows and resorted the table, 40% of your costs are wrong — but no errors appear. The formula is =VLOOKUP(A2, Costs!A:D, 4).
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause, and the robust fix?
choices: The missing 4th argument defaults range_lookup to TRUE (approximate match), which requires sorted data and returns the nearest lower value silently. Fix: pass FALSE for exact match — better, switch to XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH which default to exact match and don't depend on column position
VLOOKUP broke because the table was resorted; re-sort it back
The supplier's new rows have trailing spaces; TRIM the lookup values
VLOOKUP can't handle tables over 1,000 rows; split the table
scenarios.why: VLOOKUP's default TRUE means 'approximate match' — on unsorted data it returns plausible-but-wrong values with no error, the most dangerous spreadsheet failure mode. Exact-match FALSE fixes it, but XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH are structurally safer: they default to exact match and reference columns by name/position independently, so inserted columns don't shift the return.
scenarios.hint: What does the omitted 4th argument default to — and what does that default assume about your data?
evidence: Explain the failure mode of VLOOKUP's default TRUE argument

scenarios.title: The Model Nobody Can Audit
scenarios.situation: You inherited a revenue forecast workbook: 12 sheets, formulas referencing cells three sheets away, hardcoded numbers inside formulas (=B4*1.07), and no documentation. The CFO asks 'where does the 1.07 come from?' and you can't answer.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation before this model is used for decisions?
choices: Rebuild it from scratch — inherited models are never trustworthy

Freeze decisions on it until audited: extract all hardcoded constants into a named Assumptions sheet, trace precedents to map the calculation flow, add checks (balance checks, reasonableness bounds), document each sheet's purpose — then get the logic re-validated by the model owner before any decision use
Just find the 1.07 and replace it with the right number
Convert it to a BI tool and the problems go away
scenarios.why: Hardcoded constants buried in formulas are unauditable assumptions — the 1.07 might be growth, inflation, or a typo. The remediation is structural: a single Assumptions sheet makes every input visible and changeable, precedent-tracing maps the logic, and check cells catch future breaks. Rebuilding wastes the embedded business logic; patching one number leaves the other hundred hidden.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a number in a formula and a number in an Assumptions sheet?
objectives: Audit and remediate an inherited spreadsheet model
evidence: List the three structural fixes for an unauditable workbook

choices: Start the y-axis at zero for bar charts (bar length encodes value); line charts for trends can zoom — truncated bar axes exaggerate tiny differences into dramatic gaps
Truncated axes are always fine
Bar charts should never start at zero
Axis choice doesn't affect perception
scenarios.hint: Two bars: 98 vs 100. With the axis starting at 95, how big does the difference look?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the y-axis baseline matter?
scenarios.situation: A bar chart with the y-axis starting at 90 makes a 2% difference look like a 10x gap. Marketing loves it.
scenarios.title: The dramatic bar chart
scenarios.why: Bar length encodes value — truncating the axis breaks the encoding, turning small differences into visual lies. Bars: start at zero. Lines (position encodes value, not length) may zoom to show variation — but label clearly. The analyst's job: choose the axis that informs, not the one that impresses. When someone asks for the truncated version, show both and explain.

choices: Line chart for trends over time, bar for comparisons, scatter for relationships, histogram for distributions — and almost never pie (humans judge angles poorly)
Pie charts for everything — they're friendly
3D charts add clarity
One chart type fits all data
scenarios.hint: 'Sales over 12 months' vs 'market share' vs 'price vs demand' — which shape answers each?
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose the chart type?
scenarios.situation: A deck uses pie charts for trends, 3D bars for comparisons, and a table for a distribution.
scenarios.title: The chart-type roulette
scenarios.why: Match encoding to question: trends over time → line; categorical comparison → bar; two-variable relationship → scatter; distribution shape → histogram; part-of-whole (few parts) → stacked bar beats pie (angle judgment is weak; length judgment is strong). 3D distorts every encoding it touches. The chart is an argument — pick the one that makes the true pattern easiest to see.

choices: Direct labels / annotations on the chart — put the numbers where the eye already is; legends force eye-tennis between chart and key
Legends are mandatory for all charts
Colors alone communicate values
Annotations clutter charts
scenarios.hint: With 8 similar colors and a legend, how long does it take to find 'Northeast'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make a multi-series chart readable?
scenarios.situation: An 8-region line chart with a legend: readers can't tell which line is which.
scenarios.title: The legend hunt
scenarios.why: Direct labeling (series names at line ends, values on bars) removes the legend-lookup round trip — the eye stays on the data. Legends fail past ~4 similar series. Annotate the insight too ('Launch spike', 'Policy change') — a chart without the 'so what' labeled is a puzzle, not a message. Reduce the reader's work to zero.

choices: Colorblind-safe palettes, sufficient contrast, never color-as-only-encoding (add labels/patterns) — ~8% of men have color-vision deficiency
Rainbow palettes maximize information
Red-green is fine; everyone sees it
Accessibility doesn't apply to internal dashboards
scenarios.hint: If red and green look identical to the reader, what does your 'good vs bad' encoding say?
scenarios.prompt: What are the color rules for dashboards?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard encodes good/bad as red/green only. A colorblind stakeholder misreads it.
scenarios.title: The red-green dashboard
scenarios.why: ~1 in 12 men has color-vision deficiency — red/green as the sole encoding excludes them. Rules: colorblind-safe palettes (blue/orange, not red/green), color never the only channel (add labels, shapes, or position), sufficient contrast for text. Accessibility isn't polish; it's correctness for part of your audience.

choices: Small multiples — same chart repeated per segment at the same scale; comparison happens visually, instantly
One chart with 20 series
Separate dashboards per segment
Animation between segments
scenarios.hint: 12 regions × monthly trend — one spaghetti chart, or 12 small identical charts?
scenarios.prompt: How do you compare many segments?
scenarios.situation: A 20-series line chart is spaghetti. Splitting into 20 slides loses comparison.
scenarios.title: The spaghetti chart
scenarios.why: Small multiples: the same chart repeated per segment, identical scales, in a grid — the eye compares shapes instantly. One overloaded chart is unreadable; separate pages break comparison. Same scale is the discipline (different scales lie). For segment comparison, small multiples are the most information-dense honest layout.

choices: Declutter: remove gridlines/borders/3D, highlight the data (one accent color for the insight, gray for context), maximize data-ink ratio
More elements look more professional
Every chart needs a border and background shading
Data-ink ratio is aesthetic trivia
scenarios.hint: What remains when you delete everything that isn't data?
scenarios.prompt: What is the decluttering discipline?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard is heavy borders, gridlines, gradients, and 3D — the data is hard to find.
scenarios.title: The chartjunk
scenarios.why: Data-ink ratio: maximize ink spent on data, minimize on decoration. Remove: heavy gridlines, borders, backgrounds, 3D effects, redundant labels. Then highlight: one accent color draws the eye to the insight; everything else recedes to gray. A clean chart isn't minimalism for style — it's respect for the reader's attention.

scenarios.title: The Chart That Cried Crisis
scenarios.situation: Your churn dashboard shows a dramatic spike — the line shoots up in March. The VP is alarmed. You check: the y-axis starts at 4.2% and ends at 5.1%, and March included a one-time data backfill of previously uncounted cancellations.
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the visualization and communicate the finding?
choices: Keep the chart as-is; the spike is real data
Remove March from the data so the trend looks clean
Switch to a bar chart, which makes spikes look less dramatic
Fix the axis to start at zero (or show full context), annotate the March backfill directly on the chart, and lead with 'no real spike — a backfill artifact' before showing the corrected trend
scenarios.why: A truncated axis turned a 0.9pp wobble into a visual crisis, and the backfill made it a data artifact, not a business event. The fix is two-part: honest scaling plus annotation of the anomaly's cause ON the chart (so the context travels with the image). Leading with the conclusion prevents the VP from acting on the first impression.
scenarios.hint: What would this chart look like with a zero baseline — and what caused March, really?
objectives: Apply honest axis scaling and annotate data artifacts
evidence: Explain why the annotation must live on the chart, not in the email body

scenarios.title: Dashboard or Data Dump?
scenarios.situation: Your sales dashboard has 14 charts, 6 KPI cards, and 3 filters. Usage analytics show managers open it, stare, and close it — then ask you for the numbers in Slack. The dashboard 'has everything' but answers nothing.
scenarios.prompt: How do you redesign it so managers actually use it?
choices: Interview 3 managers on the ONE decision the dashboard should support, rebuild around a single headline metric with 2-3 diagnostic breakdowns, push detail to drill-throughs, and delete everything that doesn't serve that decision — then watch usage, not opinions
Add more charts — they're probably missing the one they need
Make it prettier with better colors and branding
Split it into 14 separate dashboards, one per chart
scenarios.why: The dashboard failed because it was organized around data availability, not a decision. Usage analytics are the evidence: opens-without-action means cognitive overload. One decision → one headline → diagnostic layers matches how managers think (is it OK? if not, why?). Deletion is the design tool; drill-throughs preserve detail without cluttering the landing view.
scenarios.hint: What decision is a manager supposed to make within 30 seconds of opening this?
objectives: Redesign dashboards around decisions, not data availability
evidence: State the one decision your redesigned dashboard supports

choices: Median (robust to skew) alongside the mean — report both, and show the distribution; the mean alone lies about skewed data
Mean is always the right 'average'
Drop the outliers to fix the mean
Median hides information
evidence: data
Salaries: 45k, 52k, 48k, 55k, 50k, 47k, 2.5M (CEO)  →  mean ≈ 400k, median = 50k
scenarios.hint: Which single number describes 'the typical employee's salary' here?
scenarios.prompt: Which average, and why does the choice matter?
scenarios.situation: 'Average salary is $400k!' — the mean includes the CEO's $2.5M. Employees are confused.
scenarios.title: The $400k average
scenarios.why: The mean is pulled by skew; the median (50th percentile) resists it. For skewed distributions (income, home prices, deal sizes), the median describes the typical case; the mean describes the total-per-head. Report both + the distribution shape. Choosing the mean for skewed data isn't wrong math — it's wrong communication.

choices: Correlation ≠ causation — ice-cream sales correlate with drownings (both rise in summer); look for confounders, and test with experiments
Correlation proves causation with enough data
Confounders don't matter with big data
A/B tests are unnecessary when correlation is strong
scenarios.hint: What third variable rises in summer alongside both ice cream and drownings?
scenarios.prompt: What is the analytical failure?
scenarios.situation: 'Users who use feature X retain better!' — the team ships more X. Retention doesn't move. Power users adopt every feature.
scenarios.title: The feature fallacy
scenarios.why: Correlation: X-users retain more. Causation would need: X causes retention. The confounder: power users both adopt features and retain — X is a marker of engagement, not its cause. Before acting on correlation: name plausible confounders, segment (does X help within engagement bands?), and run an experiment. Observational wins are hypotheses, not conclusions.

choices: Randomized A/B test with a pre-registered metric, sufficient sample size/power, and a fixed runtime — then check statistical significance, not just the raw lift
Ship it; the 5% lift is obvious
Run the test until it looks significant, then stop
Sample size doesn't matter with a big lift
scenarios.hint: If you peek daily and stop when it's significant, what happens to your false-positive rate?
scenarios.prompt: How do you run the test properly?
scenarios.situation: A button change shows +5% conversion after 3 days. The team wants to ship; nobody computed power or significance.
scenarios.title: The 5% lift
scenarios.why: Proper A/B: randomize, pre-register the primary metric and runtime, size for statistical power (enough users to detect a meaningful effect), then read significance at the end. Sins: peeking/stopping early (inflates false positives), tiny samples (noise), and multiple metrics without correction (one will 'win' by chance). +5% on 200 users is noise; on 200k it's signal. Do the math before shipping.

choices: Selection bias — survey respondents self-select (happy/angry extremes); the sample doesn't represent all users. Weight, or better, sample randomly
Survey results are representative by default
More responses fix bias
Bias only matters in small samples
scenarios.hint: Who bothers to answer a satisfaction survey — the delighted, the furious, or the indifferent middle?
scenarios.prompt: Why might the 4.8/5 satisfaction score be misleading?
scenarios.situation: A satisfaction survey (2% response rate) scores 4.8/5, but churn is rising and support tickets grow.
scenarios.title: The 4.8 paradox
scenarios.why: 2% response = self-selected extremes; the indifferent middle (often the churners) doesn't answer. The score measures 'respondents', not 'users'. Fixes: random sampling with follow-up, compare respondent vs population characteristics, weight responses, and triangulate with behavioral data (tickets, churn). A biased sample doesn't improve with size — 100k biased responses are still biased.

choices: Base rates — 1% defect rate means most positives are false positives even with a '99% accurate' test; always combine test accuracy with the base rate (Bayes)
99% accurate means 99% of positives are true
Base rates don't matter with good tests
False positives are rare by definition
evidence: math

1000 shipments, 1% truly late (10). Test: 99% accurate.
→ ~10 true positives + ~10 false positives → P(late | flagged) ≈ 50%
scenarios.hint: Out of 1000 shipments with 10 truly late, how many false alarms does a 99%-accurate flag raise?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the '99% accurate' alert wrong half the time?
scenarios.situation: A '99% accurate' late-shipment predictor flags orders; half the flags are wrong. The team blames the model.
scenarios.title: The base-rate trap
scenarios.why: With a 1% base rate, even 99% accuracy yields ~equal true and false positives (10 real lates caught, ~10 false alarms from 990 on-time). P(late|flagged) ≈ 50%. The model is fine; the expectation ignored Bayes. Lesson: rare-event prediction needs either much higher precision or a workflow that tolerates false alarms. Always condition on the base rate.

choices: Simpson's paradox — the aggregate reverses the segment trends; segment before concluding (e.g., by traffic source/device)
Aggregates are always trustworthy
The segments must be wrong
Paradoxes don't occur in real data
evidence: data

Overall: new design converts better (5% vs 4%).
By segment: old design wins on mobile AND on desktop.
scenarios.hint: What if the new design got 90% desktop traffic (high-converting) and the old got 90% mobile?
scenarios.prompt: How can the new design win overall but lose in every segment?
scenarios.situation: Overall conversion favors the new design, but it loses within mobile and within desktop separately.
scenarios.title: The paradox
scenarios.why: Simpson's paradox: a lurking variable (traffic mix) reverses the aggregate. If the new design received mostly high-converting desktop traffic, its overall rate is inflated by mix, not merit. Within each segment, the old design wins. Rule: always segment by known confounders (device, source, region) before trusting an aggregate — the overall number can lie while every segment tells the truth.

scenarios.title: The Average That Hid the Story
scenarios.situation: Average order value is flat year-over-year at $82, and leadership is relieved. But you notice the distribution: a growing mass of $15 orders and a shrinking set of $400 orders. The business mix is transforming under a flat mean.
scenarios.prompt: What analysis do you present instead of the flat average?
choices: Report the median instead — it's more robust
The average is the KPI; report it as flat and move on

Show the distribution: segment AOV by customer cohort/order-size bands over time, revealing the barbell shift (volume up in small orders, value leaking from large ones) — the flat mean is two opposing trends canceling, and the business question is which trend to feed
Remove the $400 outliers so the average reflects 'typical' orders
scenarios.why: A flat mean can hide a structural transformation — this is the business version of Simpson's paradox territory. Segmenting by order-size bands over time reveals the barbell: the company is becoming a different business. The median alone would also move oddly. Leadership needs the distribution story because 'feed the $15 segment' and 'save the $400 segment' are opposite strategies.
scenarios.hint: What two opposing trends can sum to a flat line — and which one should the business feed?
objectives: Replace single means with distributional analysis
evidence: Sketch the segmented view that reveals the barbell shift

scenarios.title: Correlation in the Board Deck
scenarios.situation: Your analysis shows a 0.85 correlation between support ticket volume and churn. The CPO wants to put 'reducing tickets reduces churn' in the board deck as a strategic pillar. You know tickets and churn both spike after the same buggy releases.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the CPO's request?
choices: Approve it — 0.85 is a strong correlation and directionally right
Refuse to present any correlational finding ever again
Weaken the language to 'associated with' and let the board infer causation

Push back with the confounder: both are driven by release quality, so cutting tickets (e.g., by hiding the support button) won't cut churn. Propose the testable version: instrument release quality as the lever, and suggest an experiment (staged rollout) to establish causation before it becomes strategy
scenarios.why: This is the classic confounder: buggy releases cause both tickets and churn, so the correlation is real but the causal claim is false — acting on it (suppress tickets) could even increase churn. The analyst's duty is to block the causal leap while offering the path forward: name the confounder, propose the real lever, and design the experiment that would earn the board-level claim.
scenarios.hint: What third variable moves both tickets and churn — and what happens if you 'fix' tickets without touching it?
objectives: Block confounded causal claims; propose experimental validation
evidence: Name the confounder and the experiment that would test the real lever

choices: Semantic layer — define each metric once (SQL/model), certify it, and have every dashboard consume the definition; 'revenue' has one author and one meaning
Each dashboard defines its own metrics — flexibility
Semantic layers slow down analysis
One definition per dashboard is fine
scenarios.hint: Who decides what 'active user' means — each dashboard author, or one governed definition?
scenarios.prompt: How do you end 'three dashboards, three revenues'?
scenarios.situation: Three dashboards show three different revenue numbers. Each defines revenue slightly differently.
scenarios.title: The three revenues
scenarios.why: A semantic layer centralizes metric definitions: one governed 'revenue' (with its exact logic, filters, and grain), consumed by all dashboards and self-service. Dashboards become presentations of certified metrics, not independent computations. Without it, every dashboard is a new opinion. With it, arguments move from 'whose number is right' to 'is the definition right' — a much better argument.

choices: Aggregate/navigation design: pre-aggregate at common grains, limit default date ranges, push filters to the source, and monitor query performance — dashboards must feel instant
Load raw billions of rows into the dashboard
Performance is the warehouse's problem
Users tolerate 2-minute dashboard loads
scenarios.hint: A dashboard scanning 5B rows per load — what computes once instead of per-view?
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep dashboards fast over big data?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard over billions of rows takes 90 seconds to load. Users stop using it.
scenarios.title: The 90-second dashboard
scenarios.why: Dashboard performance discipline: pre-aggregate to the dashboard's grain (materialized/aggregate tables), default to sane date ranges (not 'all time'), ensure filters hit partitioned/indexed columns, and cache. A dashboard is a serving layer — it should query aggregates, not raw fact tables. If the dashboard queries billions of rows per interaction, the modeling failed, not the tool.

choices: Certified vs sandbox: governed, certified datasets for official metrics; sandbox/exploratory space for ad-hoc work — with clear labeling so nobody mistakes one for the other
All self-service, no governance — fastest
Lock everything down — no self-service
Governance and self-service are opposites
scenarios.hint: How do you let analysts explore freely without letting experiments become 'official numbers'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you balance self-service with trust?
scenarios.situation: Analysts build on raw tables; executives quote exploratory numbers as fact. Locking everything down kills productivity.
scenarios.title: The wild-west BI
scenarios.why: Two-tier: certified datasets (governed, documented, tested — the official numbers) and a sandbox (raw/exploratory — clearly labeled 'unverified'). Analysts explore freely in the sandbox; promotion to certified requires review. Labeling is the keystone: every dashboard states its certification status. Self-service without governance produces confident wrong numbers; governance without self-service produces shadow BI.

choices: Row-level security — filter data by the viewer's identity/role in the BI tool or semantic layer; one dashboard, many views, enforced centrally
One dashboard per team — simplest secure
RLS is just hiding tabs
Security can be handled by telling users not to look
scenarios.hint: The CEO and a regional manager open the same dashboard — who should see whose numbers?
scenarios.prompt: How does one dashboard serve many audiences securely?
scenarios.situation: A sales dashboard must show each rep only their territory, managers their region, execs everything.
scenarios.title: The one-dashboard rule
scenarios.why: Row-level security applies data filters by viewer identity (role, territory mapping) — one dashboard definition, personalized data, enforced in the platform (not in the user's hands). Cloning dashboards per audience multiplies maintenance and leaks via stale copies. RLS belongs in the semantic layer/platform so it's consistent across every surface.

choices: Scheduled refresh aligned to data SLAs + data-driven alerts (alert when a metric crosses a threshold, not just 'dashboard updated') — push the insight, don't just publish it
Refresh everything hourly — fresher is always better
Alerts on every data change
Manual refresh is fine
scenarios.hint: Nobody opens the dashboard — how does the insight reach them?
scenarios.prompt: How do dashboards stay fresh and actually seen?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard refreshes nightly, but the metric it tracks moves intraday. Nobody checks it anyway.
scenarios.title: The unseen dashboard
scenarios.why: Match refresh to the data's SLA and decision cadence (intraday metric → intraday refresh; daily KPI → daily). Then invert the model: data-driven alerts push exceptions to stakeholders (Slack/email when churn spikes) instead of hoping they open the dashboard. Dashboards are for investigation; alerts are for attention. An unopened dashboard is a write-only report.

choices: Version the dashboard definitions, document metric logic, and review changes — dashboards are code; treat them like it
Dashboards don't need version control
Screenshots document dashboards
Only the data needs governance
scenarios.hint: Who changed the revenue filter last Tuesday, and can you get the old version back?
scenarios.prompt: How do you operate dashboards like software?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard's numbers change; nobody knows who edited it or what changed.
scenarios.title: The mystery edit
scenarios.why: Dashboards are production artifacts: version their definitions (BI tools with git integration, or exported definitions in version control), document metric logic alongside, require review for certified dashboards, and keep a changelog. 'Someone edited the filter' shouldn't be a mystery — it should be a commit. Operate dashboards with the same discipline as the pipelines feeding them.

scenarios.title: Two Dashboards, Two Truths
scenarios.situation: Marketing's dashboard says Q3 leads were 12,400; Sales' dashboard says 9,800. Both pull from the warehouse. Marketing counts every form fill; Sales counts only leads with valid emails that weren't duplicates. Leadership asks you for 'the number'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct resolution?
choices: Pick the Sales number — it's more conservative and finance likes it
Average them and note the methodology difference

Don't pick — define the metric once in a shared semantic layer: document each definition (raw fills vs qualified leads), get stakeholder sign-off on which definition answers which question, implement both as named, certified metrics, and deprecate the conflicting dashboards
Tell leadership the data is unreliable and stop reporting leads
scenarios.why: There is no single 'true' number — there are two valid definitions answering different questions. The failure is governance, not data: conflicting definitions in separate dashboards. A semantic layer (certified metrics with documented logic) makes the definition the product, signed off once and reused everywhere. Picking or averaging hides the real disagreement.
scenarios.hint: Is the disagreement about the data, or about what the word 'leads' means?
objectives: Resolve metric conflicts with a governed semantic layer
evidence: Write the one-paragraph definition for each of the two lead metrics

scenarios.title: The Dashboard That Times Out
scenarios.situation: Your executive dashboard times out every Monday morning. It runs 8 live queries against raw event tables (2B rows), each scanning full partitions. The execs need it by 9 AM; the data team says 'the warehouse is slow on Mondays'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct architectural fix?
choices: Buy a bigger warehouse — compute solves timeouts
Tell the execs to open the dashboard on Tuesday instead
Cache the dashboard in the BI tool and hope the cache holds

Move the heavy lifting out of the dashboard: pre-aggregate the executive metrics into a scheduled mart (hourly/daily), so the dashboard queries thousands of rows instead of billions; keep live queries only for drill-downs, and set refresh expectations explicitly (data as of 8 AM, not real-time)
scenarios.why: Live dashboards over raw event tables re-scan billions of rows per viewer per load — the architecture is the bug. Pre-aggregation (a scheduled mart) converts the dashboard query from a 2B-row scan to a small lookup; it's also deterministic (same numbers for everyone) and cheap. 'Bigger warehouse' treats the symptom at full price. The refresh contract ('as of 8 AM') kills the real-time expectation that caused the design.
scenarios.hint: How many times is the same 2B-row aggregation being recomputed — once, or once per viewer per Monday?
objectives: Architect BI with pre-aggregated marts behind live dashboards
evidence: State the refresh contract you'd set with the execs

choices: Pyramid principle — lead with the conclusion/recommendation, then supporting evidence, then details; executives decide, they don't explore
Build suspense: background, methodology, then the answer on slide 20
Chronological order is clearest
Details first, conclusion last
scenarios.hint: The exec has 2 minutes — do they get the answer first or last?
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure findings for decision-makers?
scenarios.situation: A 30-slide deck buries the recommendation on slide 28. The exec stops paying attention at slide 5.
scenarios.title: The buried lede
scenarios.why: Pyramid principle: answer first ('We should do X'), then the 2-3 supporting reasons, then details as backup. Executives need the decision up front; they drill into evidence only where they doubt. Chronological 'here's what I did' structures serve the analyst's journey, not the reader's decision. Lead with the 'so what', earn the right to the 'how'.

choices: One message per chart, stated in the title — 'Churn spikes after the price increase' not 'Churn by month'; the title is the takeaway
Cute titles: 'Churn analysis'
Titles should describe the chart type
Takeaways belong in the appendix
scenarios.hint: Does the title tell the reader what to conclude, or just what the chart shows?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a chart title effective?
scenarios.situation: A deck of charts titled 'Revenue by segment', 'Churn by month' — readers must deduce each point themselves.
scenarios.title: The descriptive titles
scenarios.why: Action titles state the insight ('Enterprise churn doubled after onboarding changes'), not the content ('Churn by segment'). Each chart makes one point; the title is that point. Descriptive titles outsource interpretation to the busiest readers — they'll get it wrong or skip it. Write the title last, after you know the message.

choices: Show the uncertainty: ranges, confidence intervals, sensitivity ('if X, then Y') — and state what would change the conclusion; false precision destroys trust when you're wrong
Point estimates only — ranges look indecisive
Hide the caveats; they'll ask if needed
Uncertainty means the analysis failed
scenarios.hint: 'Revenue will grow 12%' vs 'likely 8–15%, driven by enterprise renewals' — which survives being slightly wrong?
scenarios.prompt: How do you present uncertain findings honestly?
scenarios.situation: A forecast is presented as a single number. It's wrong; stakeholders stop trusting the team's numbers.
scenarios.title: The false precision
scenarios.why: Honest uncertainty: ranges instead of point estimates, key assumptions stated, sensitivity to drivers ('±3 points if renewal rate moves 5%'), and pre-mortem ('what would change this conclusion'). False precision borrows trust and repays it with interest when wrong. Decision-makers can act on ranges; they can't act on a number nobody believes.

choices: Context → complication → resolution: set the business context, name the tension, then the recommendation — a narrative arc, not a data dump
Data dump in appendix order
Start with methodology — credibility first
Narratives are for marketing, not analysis
scenarios.hint: 'Sales are flat' (context), 'but enterprise is collapsing while SMB grows' (tension) — what's the resolution?
scenarios.prompt: How do you turn analysis into a story?
scenarios.situation: A readout lists 15 findings. Stakeholders remember none and ask 'so what do we do?'
scenarios.title: The 15 findings
scenarios.why: Narrative arc: context (what's happening), complication (the tension/change), resolution (what we should do). Fifteen findings with no arc = fifteen forgettable facts. Group findings into 2-3 insights that build to one recommendation. Stories are memory structures — the same data, shaped as tension→resolution, gets remembered and acted on.

choices: Recommendation tied to evidence with trade-offs named: 'Do X because [evidence]; costs [Y]; if [assumption] is wrong, do Z' — a decision, not a suggestion
'Further analysis needed' — safest close
Recommendations without trade-offs
Let stakeholders decide; analysts shouldn't recommend
scenarios.hint: Does the close tell them what to do Monday morning, or just what you found?
scenarios.prompt: How do you close an analysis?
scenarios.situation: A readout ends with 'interesting patterns'. No decision is made; the work dies.
scenarios.title: The inconclusive close
scenarios.why: Close with a recommendation: the action, the evidence behind it, the trade-offs/costs, and the tripwire ('revisit if X'). 'Further analysis needed' is sometimes honest but usually abdication — say what the current evidence supports and what would change your mind. Analysis exists to drive decisions; a readout without a recommendation is entertainment.

choices: Pre-wire: share findings with key stakeholders before the big meeting, gather objections privately, adjust — the meeting ratifies, it doesn't discover
Surprise everyone in the meeting — impact
Pre-wiring is politics, not analysis
Only present to friendly audiences
scenarios.hint: The VP objects to your methodology in front of 20 people — when should that conversation have happened?
scenarios.prompt: How do you land a controversial finding?
scenarios.situation: A finding ('the flagship feature hurts retention') blindsides its owner in a big review. The meeting derails into methodology debate.
scenarios.title: The ambush
scenarios.why: Pre-wire controversial findings: walk key stakeholders through the analysis 1:1 before the forum — hear objections, stress-test the logic, adjust where they're right. The big meeting then decides rather than discovers. An ambush triggers defensiveness; a pre-wired finding gets a fair hearing. It's not politics — it's giving the analysis its best chance to be judged on merit.

scenarios.title: The 40-Slide Deck
scenarios.situation: You have a 40-slide deck for the pricing analysis: methodology, 25 charts, appendices. In the dry run, the VP checks out by slide 6. The insight — a 3% price increase on the mid tier adds $2M with <1% churn risk — is on slide 34.
scenarios.prompt: How do you restructure the story?
choices: Cut it to 20 slides — shorter is always better

Pyramid structure: lead with the recommendation and the $2M (slide 1), then the 3 supporting evidence blocks (demand elasticity, churn modeling, competitive check), then methodology as backup — the 25 charts become an appendix; every slide must earn its place by supporting the recommendation
Present all 40 slides faster so you finish in time
Send the deck in advance and skip the meeting
scenarios.why: Executives decide top-down: recommendation first, then the minimum evidence to trust it. The 40-slide chronological dump forces them to do the analyst's synthesis work. The pyramid (answer → arguments → evidence) respects their time; the appendix preserves rigor for the one person who'll ask. 'Shorter' without structure just hides the insight faster.
scenarios.hint: What does the VP need to decide — and what is the minimum they must believe to decide it?
objectives: Structure executive stories with the pyramid principle
evidence: Write the slide-1 headline for this pricing story

scenarios.title: Prewiring the Tough Finding
scenarios.situation: Your analysis shows the flagship product line — the CEO's pet project — is losing money on every unit after true cost allocation. Dropping this in the quarterly review will blindside leadership and trigger defensiveness.
scenarios.prompt: How do you deliver a finding that threatens a pet project?
choices: Soften the numbers so it's less confrontational
Present it cold — the data speaks for itself

Prewire: share the methodology and draft findings 1:1 with key stakeholders before the meeting, stress-test the cost allocation with finance first, frame around options (fix pricing, cut costs, sunset) not verdicts, and let no one be surprised in the room
Bury it in the appendix and mention it briefly
scenarios.why: Surprise converts analytical findings into political fights. Prewiring 1:1s lets stakeholders process, challenge the methodology privately (where you can fix real issues), and arrive at the meeting ready to discuss options. Validating allocation with finance first removes the easiest attack vector. Framing as options ('here are three paths') keeps the analyst in advisory role, not executioner.
scenarios.hint: What happens in the room if the CEO hears this for the first time on slide 12?
objectives: Deliver threatening findings via prewiring and options framing
evidence: List who you prewire and in what order

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Data Analyst as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The SQL for Analysis Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that SQL for Analysis is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in SQL for Analysis?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — SQL for Analysis issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — SQL for Analysis is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is SQL for Analysis supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any SQL for Analysis failure in Data Analyst.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to SQL for Analysis
evidence: System Status
All SQL for Analysis components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The Spreadsheets Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Spreadsheets is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Spreadsheets?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Spreadsheets issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Spreadsheets is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Spreadsheets supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Spreadsheets failure in Data Analyst.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
evidence: System Status
All Spreadsheets components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Pipeline Anatomy: The Stale Dashboard
scenarios.situation: The revenue dashboard shows yesterday's numbers at noon — 12 hours stale. The pipeline is: app DB → CDC → stream → warehouse → dbt models → BI extract. Each stage's owner says 'my part is green'.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the data's journey — where do you look, and in what order?
choices: Trace forward with watermarks: check the warehouse's latest loaded timestamp per source (did fresh data arrive?), then dbt's last successful run and its max processed timestamp (did the model advance?), then the BI extract's refresh time — the break is at the first stage whose watermark stopped advancing, and 'green' stage health doesn't prove data flowed
Restart the BI extract; it's the last stage so it's probably the problem
Rebuild the whole pipeline — stale data means systemic failure
Ask each owner again more firmly
scenarios.why: Trace the journey with watermarks, not status lights: a stage can be 'green' (process running) while processing nothing (upstream empty, or a silent filter dropping rows). The max-timestamp watermark at each handoff pinpoints the stall — data arrived at the warehouse but dbt's model watermark is 12h old? The break is the dbt run. Systems thinking: follow the artifact (data), not the dashboard (opinions).
scenarios.hint: What timestamp does each stage stamp on the data — and which one stopped moving?
objectives: Trace pipeline stalls using watermark evidence
Distinguish process health from data flow
evidence: Name the watermark to check at each of the 5 handoffs

scenarios.title: BI Stack Flow: The Slow Filter
scenarios.situation: A BI dashboard is fast for the default view but takes 90 seconds when a user picks a specific region. The dashboard queries a view over the orders table; the region filter is applied in the BI tool. The DBA says the table is indexed on region.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the query path — why does the filter make it slower, not faster?
choices: The BI tool wraps the view in an outer query, and the region predicate can't push through the view's aggregation — so the engine scans and aggregates ALL regions, then filters. Fix: expose region in the grouped mart (or use an aggregate-aware design) so the filter prunes partitions before aggregation
The index is corrupted; rebuild it
90 seconds is normal for filtered queries; add a loading spinner
The region has more data, so it's naturally slower
scenarios.why: Trace the query: BI generates SELECT ... FROM (view with GROUP BY) WHERE region = X. The aggregation inside the view must complete before the outer filter applies — predicate pushdown fails through the aggregation barrier, so you pay for all regions to see one. The fix moves the filter inside the aggregation's reach: partition/group by region in the mart so the engine prunes before aggregating. The index is irrelevant once the aggregation blocks the predicate.
scenarios.hint: Where does the WHERE clause sit relative to the GROUP BY in the generated SQL?
objectives: Trace BI queries through views to find pushdown failures
Design marts that let filters prune early
evidence: Sketch the generated SQL showing the filter outside the aggregation

scenarios.title: Metric Definition Chain: The Churn Dispute
scenarios.situation: Product says churn is 3%, Finance says 7%. You trace both: Product counts 'users with no login in 30 days' from the events table; Finance counts 'canceled subscriptions' from the billing table. Both queries are correct.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systems-level fix?
choices: Declare Finance correct — money is the real churn
Average them to 5% and move on

Map the full definition chain for each: event → entity → rule → window → population, then show they're measuring different things (engagement lapse vs revenue cancellation). Create two certified metrics with distinct names ('dormancy rate' vs 'subscription churn'), document the chain for each, and route each stakeholder to the right one
Rewrite both queries to use the same table
scenarios.why: Both numbers are 'correct' because they measure different phenomena through different chains: events→user→30d-no-login vs billing→subscription→cancel-event. The dispute isn't about SQL, it's about unnamed concepts sharing one word ('churn'). The fix names the chains: distinct certified names, documented entity/rule/window, each wired to the decisions it serves. Forcing one table would destroy a valid signal.
scenarios.hint: Write out each metric's full chain: what event, what entity, what rule, what window?
objectives: Resolve metric disputes by naming distinct concepts
evidence: Write the definition chain for each of the two churn numbers

scenarios.title: Dashboard Query Path: The Monday Spike
scenarios.situation: Every Monday at 9 AM the warehouse queues spike and dashboards crawl. The rest of the week is fine. The BI tool, the dbt schedule, and the data team's ad-hoc queries all hit the same warehouse.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the contention — what is the structural fix?
choices: The warehouse is undersized; scale it up every Monday
Ban ad-hoc queries on Monday mornings
It's normal; Mondays are just busy

Map the Monday 9 AM load: scheduled dbt runs + BI scheduled refreshes + humans all collide in one window. Fix structurally: stagger the schedules (dbt finishes by 7, BI refreshes 7-8, humans get 9+), isolate workloads (separate warehouse/compute for scheduled vs interactive), and move the heaviest dashboard queries to pre-aggregated marts
scenarios.why: Trace the load curve: three workload classes (batch transforms, scheduled BI, interactive humans) all scheduled for the same window by independent owners — a coordination failure, not a capacity failure. Staggering separates them in time; workload isolation separates them in compute; pre-aggregation removes the heaviest queries entirely. Scaling up pays Monday prices for a Monday-only problem.
scenarios.hint: Who scheduled what for 9 AM Monday — and did any of them know about the others?
objectives: Diagnose warehouse contention as a scheduling collision
evidence: Draw the Monday 9 AM load timeline across the three workload classes

scenarios.title: Experiment Pipeline: The Leaking Randomization
scenarios.situation: An A/B test shows the variant winning by 15%, but the variant group has 20% more mobile users than control. Randomization was 'by user ID hash'. The experiment runs across web and mobile apps.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the assignment pipeline — where did the imbalance come from?
choices: 15% is a big win; ship it — imbalance doesn't matter with large samples

Trace assignment: user ID hash → bucket, but mobile and web have different ID namespaces (a user can have two IDs), and the hash function was applied per-platform. Users crossing platforms get double-counted or mis-bucketed, and platform mix differs by acquisition channel. Fix: randomize on a stable cross-platform identity, validate balance (SRM check) before reading results, and re-run
The hash function is broken; use a different one
Exclude mobile users from the analysis
scenarios.why: Trace the unit of randomization: 'user ID' isn't one thing when web and mobile mint different IDs for the same human. Per-platform hashing breaks the exchangeability the test assumes — the 20% mobile skew IS the 15% win (mobile converts differently). The SRM (sample ratio mismatch) check exists exactly to catch this before anyone reads results. Randomize on the identity that matches the analysis unit.
scenarios.hint: What is the actual unit being randomized — and is it the same unit on web and mobile?
objectives: Trace experiment assignment to find identity fragmentation
Apply SRM checks before reading results
evidence: Explain how one human becomes two randomized units

scenarios.title: Data Quality System: The Silent Drop
scenarios.situation: Order counts drift down 2% per week for a month. No pipeline failures, no errors, all tests green. The drop is real — finance confirms revenue is down. The ingestion is: API → validation → warehouse.
scenarios.prompt: Where in the system can rows vanish without errors, and how do you find it?
choices: The tests are wrong; rewrite them
Revenue is down because of the economy, not the data

Trace row counts stage to stage: API responses → accepted by validation → written to warehouse. Silent drops live in validation rules (a new product category failing a regex, stricter schema rejecting edge cases) or in dedup logic. Instrument counts at every handoff with alerts on drift, then diff a dropped sample against the rules to find which rule eats them
Backfill the missing 8% and move on
scenarios.why: Errors are loud; validation rejections are silent by design — the system is 'working' while eating 2% of rows weekly. The drift pattern (steady %, not a cliff) points at a rule interacting with a shifting input (new category, new format), not an outage. Stage-to-stage count reconciliation is the systems instrument that makes silent drops visible; diffing rejected rows against rules names the culprit. Green tests only prove the tested paths.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a row that errors and a row that gets rejected — and which one pages anyone?
objectives: Instrument stage-to-stage reconciliation to catch silent drops
Diff rejected rows against validation rules
evidence: State the reconciliation query: counts at each handoff, grouped by week

scenarios.title: The Revenue That Doubled
scenarios.situation: Your 'revenue by category' query shows $2.1M. Finance says $1.05M. Your query joins orders to order_items to products. Finance sums the orders table directly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug, and what is the fix?
choices: Finance is wrong — the joined query has more detail so it must be right

Fan-out: joining orders→order_items multiplies order rows (one row per item), so SUM(order.amount) double/triple counts. Fix: aggregate at the right grain first (revenue per order), then join — or sum from the items table, never the parent after a one-to-many join
The products table has duplicates — deduplicate it
Use DISTINCT on the order amount
scenarios.why: Classic fan-out: one order with 3 items becomes 3 rows; SUM(order.amount) counts the order total 3 times. $2.1M vs $1.05M — suspiciously 2x, the tell of duplication. The fix is grain discipline: compute revenue at the order grain BEFORE joining (CTE/subquery), or sum the child table's amounts. DISTINCT on the amount would still be wrong if two orders share an amount. Always validate joined sums against the parent table total.
scenarios.hint: The total is 2x finance. What does joining to a child table do to parent rows?
evidence: Your query
SUM(o.amount) = $2.1M (orders JOIN order_items JOIN products)
Finance
SUM(amount) FROM orders = $1.05M
Check
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM order_items GROUP BY 1 — avg 2.0 items/order

scenarios.title: The Take-Home With No Question
scenarios.situation: You receive a take-home: a 2M-row e-commerce CSV and the prompt 'tell us something interesting.' 48 hours. You are tempted to build 12 charts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the winning approach?
choices: Build as many charts as possible — volume impresses

Profile first (15 min), pick ONE business question the data can answer (e.g., 'where is revenue leaking?'), answer it with 2-3 charts, document assumptions, add caveats and next steps — depth and judgment over volume
Build a machine learning model — advanced techniques stand out
Write a long methodology document with one chart
scenarios.why: 'Something interesting' tests judgment: can you find the question worth answering? Twelve charts signal no prioritization. One sharp business question, answered rigorously with stated assumptions and honest caveats, demonstrates exactly what the role needs: profiling discipline, business framing, and communication. The ML model on unprofiled data is a trap — garbage in, impressive-looking garbage out.
scenarios.hint: What is the hiring manager actually testing with a vague prompt?
evidence: Dataset
2M rows, 14 columns, no data dictionary, 48-hour deadline
Prompt
'Tell us something interesting about this data.'

scenarios.title: The Case Study Opener
scenarios.situation: The interviewer says: 'Our free-to-paid conversion dropped 20% last quarter. You have our event data, subscription data, and 45 minutes. Walk me through how you'd investigate.' They watch how you start.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest opening to this case?
choices: Immediately query the data to see the conversion trend by week
Build a dashboard of conversion metrics to explore visually
Ask for the answer — maybe they already know what happened

Clarify and scope first: confirm the metric definition and denominator, segment the drop (cohort? platform? plan? geography?), list hypotheses (acquisition mix shift, product change, tracking break, seasonality), then propose the cut order — showing structured thinking before touching data
scenarios.why: Case interviews test structured thinking, not query speed. The opener that wins: scope the metric (conversion of WHAT over WHAT), segment before explaining (a 20% drop concentrated in one cohort is a different case than a broad decline), and enumerate hypotheses including data-quality ones (tracking breaks cause 'drops' constantly). Querying first looks busy but directionless.
scenarios.hint: What are the three ways a '20% drop' can be misleading before you even query?
objectives: Open case studies with scoping, segmentation, and hypotheses
evidence: List your hypothesis set including one data-quality hypothesis

scenarios.title: SQL Whiteboard: The Gaps Problem
scenarios.situation: Whiteboard prompt: 'Find users who were active 3 months in a row.' Table: user_activity(user_id, activity_month). The interviewer wants to see your approach, not just syntax.
scenarios.prompt: What approach do you present?
choices: Self-join the table three times on consecutive months
Write a cursor that loops through each user's months

Narrate the pattern: use LAG/LEAD or row_number over a dense month sequence per user to detect 3 consecutive months — e.g., row_number partitioned by user ordered by month, then check month - row_number is constant for consecutive runs (the gaps-and-islands trick). Explain WHY it works, then write it
Say you'd do it in Python instead
scenarios.why: The interviewer is testing pattern recognition: consecutive-sequence problems are gaps-and-islands, solved by the month-minus-row_number invariant. Narrating the invariant BEFORE writing proves understanding; the triple self-join works but signals brute force. Whiteboard SQL is scored on approach communication — 'here's the trick and why it holds' beats silent correct syntax.
scenarios.hint: What stays constant across consecutive months if you subtract a running row number?
objectives: Recognize and explain gaps-and-islands patterns on a whiteboard
evidence: State the invariant that identifies a consecutive run

scenarios.title: Take-Home Critique Defense
scenarios.situation: You submitted a take-home analysis. In the review, the interviewer says: 'Your conclusion relies on this segment, but n=40 there. And you didn't address seasonality.' Your heart sinks — they're right on both.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the critique?
choices: Defend the analysis — changing your answer looks weak

Own both gaps explicitly, quantify their impact ('with n=40 the CI spans X, so the segment claim is directional at best'), propose the concrete fix for each (pool with adjacent segments or widen the window; add year-over-year controls), and reframe: 'here's what I'd do with another day' — handling critique well IS the test
Blame the dataset they provided
Promise to redo the whole take-home overnight
scenarios.why: The critique session tests intellectual honesty, not perfection — every take-home has gaps under time pressure. Owning them with quantified impact shows statistical maturity; proposing concrete fixes shows craft; the 'another day' reframe shows prioritization judgment. Defensiveness or blame-shifting fails the actual assessment, which is 'can we trust this person's judgment?'
scenarios.hint: What is the interviewer really testing — your first draft, or what you do when it's challenged?
objectives: Handle take-home critiques with owned gaps and quantified impact
evidence: Quantify the uncertainty from n=40 in one sentence

scenarios.title: The Stakeholder Scenario
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'The VP of Sales says your churn analysis is wrong because his top account renewed. He wants the methodology changed to exclude enterprise accounts. What do you do?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest response?
choices: Validate his specific claim (check the account in the data), explain what the analysis does and doesn't claim (portfolio rate vs individual anecdote), offer to add an enterprise-cut as a SECOND view without corrupting the primary metric, and hold the methodology — changing definitions per stakeholder destroys trust in the numbers
Exclude enterprise accounts — the VP owns the relationship
Redo the analysis his way to keep the peace
Escalate to your manager immediately
scenarios.why: This tests backbone with diplomacy. The anecdote-vs-rate distinction is the analytical core: one renewal doesn't move a portfolio metric. Checking his account shows respect; the second view gives him what he needs without corrupting the certified metric; holding the line protects every future analysis. Caving teaches stakeholders that pressure edits the numbers.
scenarios.hint: What does his anecdote actually prove about the portfolio rate — and what can you give him without breaking the metric?
objectives: Defend methodology under stakeholder pressure with second-view compromises
evidence: State the anecdote-vs-rate distinction in one sentence

scenarios.title: Salary Negotiation
scenarios.situation: You've passed all rounds for a Senior Data Analyst role. The offer is $115K; your research says the band is $120-140K for this market and your skills. The recruiter says 'this is the top of what we can do' and wants an answer by Friday.
scenarios.prompt: How do you negotiate?
choices: Counter with evidence, not feelings: cite the market band and your specific differentiators, ask 'what would it take to get to $130K?' to test whether it's a real constraint, negotiate the full package (sign-on, remote flexibility, review timeline) — and never accept a exploding deadline without one extension ask
Accept — pushing back risks the offer
Counter at $140K and threaten to walk
Accept verbally then keep interviewing for leverage
scenarios.why: The 'top of what we can do' is usually the top of what they've OFFERED, not the band — the diagnostic question ('what would it take?') reveals whether it's policy or posture. Evidence-based counters (band data + your differentiators) keep it professional. The full package matters: a $10K sign-on or 6-month salary review can beat a base stalemate. One extension ask is standard; exploding deadlines are pressure tactics.
scenarios.hint: What question distinguishes a real budget cap from a negotiating posture?
objectives: Negotiate offers with evidence and package thinking
evidence: Write the one question that tests whether the cap is real

scenarios.title: Presenting Your Portfolio
scenarios.situation: The hiring manager asks you to walk through one portfolio project in 10 minutes. You have a churn analysis with great visuals. Last time you presented it, you spent 8 minutes on data cleaning and never reached the recommendation.
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the 10 minutes?
choices: Start from data ingestion and go chronologically — it's the honest story

3-2-3-2 structure: 3 min business question + your recommendation, 2 min key evidence (the 2 charts that carry it), 3 min methodology highlights (the hard parts: the join grain fix, the confounder you caught), 2 min impact + what you'd do next — cleaning gets one sentence unless asked
Show every chart — volume proves effort
Skip to the recommendation with no context to save time
scenarios.why: The manager is buying judgment, not labor. Leading with question + recommendation respects their time and frames everything after as support. Methodology highlights should showcase decisions (the grain fix, the confounder catch) — that's what distinguishes a senior. Chronological cleaning narratives bury the thinking under plumbing; one sentence ('cleaned 4 sources, handled the fan-out') suffices until probed.
scenarios.hint: What is the manager actually evaluating — your effort, or your judgment?
objectives: Present portfolio projects in recommendation-first structure
evidence: Write your one-sentence data-cleaning summary
