scenarios.title: The Pivot Table That Lied
scenarios.situation: A stakeholder's pivot shows regional revenue summing correctly, but the 'average deal size' column looks wrong — it is much lower than the CRM's figure. The pivot averages the 'deal size' column.
scenarios.prompt: What is the error?
choices: The pivot cache is stale — refresh it

Average of averages: the pivot averages per-row deal sizes, but rows have different weights (a $1M deal and a $1k deal count equally). Correct: SUM(revenue)/COUNT(deals) at the right grain, or use the data model with proper measures
The CRM is wrong — trust the pivot
A filter is hiding rows — clear all filters
scenarios.why: Averaging an already-averaged column double-averages: ten $1k deals and one $1M deal average to ~$92k per row, but the true average deal is $1.01M/11 ≈ $92k... wait, that matches here. The real trap: if the source column itself contains averages (e.g., 'avg deal size by rep'), pivoting averages those averages without weighting by deal count. Rule: never average an average without weighting. Recompute from base facts (SUM/COUNT) at the correct grain.
scenarios.hint: What is the grain of the source column? Can you average averages safely?
evidence: Pivot
Average deal size: $48k (pivot of 'deal_size' column)
CRM
Average deal size: $61k (SUM(revenue)/COUNT(closed deals))

scenarios.title: Formula vs Power Query
scenarios.situation: You get a monthly CSV (500K rows) that needs cleaning (split columns, fix dates, remove dupes), joining to a product table, and aggregating — then the whole thing repeats next month with a new file. Your current approach is 40 helper columns of formulas, and it takes 20 minutes to recalc.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tool choice?
choices: Optimize the formulas — Power Query is overkill
Move it to Python — Excel can't handle 500K rows

Rebuild as a Power Query: the steps (split, parse, dedupe, merge, group) become a recorded, replayable transformation — next month is Refresh, not rebuild. Formulas recalc cell-by-cell on 500K rows; Power Query compresses into its columnar engine and only refreshes on demand
Do the cleaning manually each month; it only takes an hour
scenarios.why: The decision rule: repeated multi-step transformations on growing data = Power Query; one-off cell logic = formulas. Power Query's value isn't speed alone — it's that the transformation is a documented, replayable pipeline (applied steps), so month 2 is a button press and the logic is auditable. 40 helper columns are 40 places for next month's errors.
scenarios.hint: What happens on the 1st of next month under each approach?
objectives: Choose Power Query for repeatable transformations over formula chains
evidence: State the decision rule for formula vs Power Query

scenarios.title: Model Design: The Forecast
scenarios.situation: You're building a 3-year revenue forecast the CFO will use for hiring plans. Drivers: headcount, price, churn, seasonality. The last forecast broke when someone inserted a row, shifting all the cell references.
scenarios.prompt: What design choices make this model robust?
choices: Build it carefully and protect the sheet so nobody inserts rows

Structure it properly: inputs on a dedicated Assumptions sheet (named ranges), calculations using structured table references (which survive row inserts), one formula pattern copied consistently down columns, checks (row totals vs column totals), and a version/date stamp — protection is the last layer, not the first
Build it in a single sheet so everything is visible
Use absolute references ($A$1) everywhere for stability
scenarios.why: Fragility came from positional references — structured table references ([@Revenue]) survive inserts because they reference by name, not address. Named assumption ranges make drivers visible and auditable. Consistent formula patterns (one formula, filled down) mean one fix fixes the column. Checks catch the breaks that slip through. Protection without structure just locks in the fragility.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when a row is inserted — and what kind of reference wouldn't?
objectives: Design robust forecast models with tables and named ranges
evidence: Explain why structured references survive row inserts

scenarios.title: Audit Findings
scenarios.situation: You audit a colleague's commission model before payout. You find: a SUM range that misses the last row (new reps added below it), a hardcoded 0.15 commission rate in 6 formulas, and a VLOOKUP with approximate match on rep IDs.
scenarios.prompt: How do you report this, and what are the fixes?
choices: Report with impact: quantify each error's dollar effect, fix structurally (convert to a Table so ranges auto-expand, move 0.15 to a named assumption, exact-match lookups), and recommend the pre-payout checklist (range-boundary check, assumption inventory, spot-check 3 reps end-to-end) so the next audit isn't needed
Fix the three issues quietly and say nothing — no harm done
Tell the colleague their model is garbage and rebuild it
Only fix the SUM — the other two are minor
scenarios.why: Audit reporting needs dollar impact — 'misses the last row' becomes '$4,200 underpaid across 3 reps', which gets attention. Structural fixes (Tables auto-expand, named assumptions, exact match) prevent recurrence; quiet patches don't. The pre-payout checklist institutionalizes the audit so correctness doesn't depend on heroics. 'Minor' issues in payout models are never minor.
scenarios.hint: What turns a bug list into action — the bug, or its dollar value?
objectives: Audit payout models and report with quantified impact
evidence: Quantify one finding's dollar impact from the scenario

scenarios.title: The 20-Minute Recalc
scenarios.situation: A pricing workbook with 300K formula cells takes 20 minutes to recalculate. It uses volatile functions (OFFSET, INDIRECT, TODAY) heavily, plus full-column references (A:A) in SUMIFS across 12 sheets.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic performance fix?
choices: Buy a faster computer for the team

Attack the calc chain: replace volatile functions (OFFSET→INDEX, INDIRECT→structured refs/CHOOSE), bound the ranges (A:A → Table columns or explicit bounds), set calculation to manual during builds, and move the heavy aggregations to Power Query/Pivot — volatiles force full recalc on EVERY change, which is the 20 minutes
Split the workbook into 12 files, one per sheet
Turn off automatic calculation permanently
scenarios.why: Volatile functions (OFFSET, INDIRECT, TODAY, NOW) recalculate on every change anywhere — 300K cells × every keystroke = the 20 minutes. Full-column refs force the engine to scan a million rows per SUMIFS. INDEX is non-volatile and precise; Tables bound ranges automatically; Power Query moves aggregation out of the calc chain entirely. Manual calc during builds is workflow, not a fix.
scenarios.hint: What recalculates on every keystroke even when its inputs didn't change?
objectives: Diagnose and fix Excel calc-chain performance
evidence: Name three volatile functions and their non-volatile replacements

scenarios.title: The Handoff
scenarios.situation: You're leaving the team and handing off a critical monthly reporting workbook to a junior analyst. It has Power Queries, pivot tables, and VBA macros. Last handoff, the successor broke it in week one by refreshing in the wrong order.
scenarios.prompt: What does a professional handoff include?
choices: A 30-minute screen-share where you click through it once
Just the file — it's self-explanatory if built well

A handoff package: a README sheet in the workbook (purpose, refresh order with dependencies, data sources + credentials owner, the 3 things that break and their fixes), a recorded walkthrough, a supervised first refresh cycle, and a 2-week shadow period — the goal is no 2 AM calls, not a fast handoff
Rewrite it without macros so there's less to explain
scenarios.why: The failure mode is known: refresh-order dependencies and tribal knowledge. A README sheet IN the workbook travels with the file (unlike emails); refresh order with dependencies prevents the week-one break; '3 things that break' pre-solves the predictable failures; supervised first cycle catches what docs miss. The shadow period is the real handoff — docs are the backup.
scenarios.hint: What broke last time — and where would the fix have needed to live to prevent it?
objectives: Execute professional workbook handoffs with runbooks
evidence: List the README sheet's required sections

scenarios.title: Data Validation Strategy
scenarios.situation: A budget template goes to 40 department heads. Returns come back with text in date fields, percentages over 100%, and department codes that don't exist. Consolidation takes you 3 days of cleanup every quarter.
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the template so consolidation is clean?
choices: Send stricter instructions with the template
Clean it faster with macros after collection
Switch to a web form — Excel can't do validation

Build validation into the template: data validation rules on every input cell (dates, 0-100%, dropdown lists for codes sourced from a master list), input messages explaining format, conditional formatting flagging violations red, a 'ready to submit' check cell that must be TRUE, and lock all non-input cells
scenarios.why: Cleanup-after is 3 days/quarter forever; validation-at-entry is a one-time build. Dropdowns from a master list eliminate bad codes structurally (can't type what isn't listed); the check cell gives submitters instant feedback instead of your angry email; locked cells prevent formula destruction. Instructions don't validate — the file must refuse bad input.
scenarios.hint: Where is the cheapest place to catch a bad department code — at entry, or in your consolidation?
objectives: Design validated input templates that eliminate cleanup
evidence: Name the four validation layers in the template

scenarios.title: Version Chaos
scenarios.situation: The forecast workbook exists as Forecast_v3_FINAL_Jan(2).xlsx, Forecast_v3_FINAL_REAL.xlsx, and three more variants across email and shared drives. Nobody knows which one the CFO saw. Two people edited different copies last week.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct version-control practice?
choices: Pick the newest file by date modified and delete the rest

Single source of truth: one file in a shared location (SharePoint/OneDrive) with version history enabled, a version log sheet inside (date, author, what changed), co-authoring instead of email copies, and a naming rule that bans FINAL — the history feature IS the version control
Merge the variants by copying the best sheets from each
It's fine — just ask the CFO which one they saw
scenarios.why: Email copies are branches with no merge strategy — divergence is guaranteed. One shared file with native version history gives you every prior state plus who-changed-what; the in-file version log makes changes human-readable; co-authoring removes the copy problem structurally. 'FINAL' in a filename is a wish, not a control.
scenarios.hint: What creates the variants — and what single change makes variants impossible?
objectives: Establish single-source version control for shared workbooks
evidence: State the rule that replaces FINAL in filenames

domains.name: A/B Testing & Experimentation
domains.description: Design valid experiments, read results honestly, and avoid the statistical traps that sink product decisions.

scenarios.title: The Experiment That 'Won' on Day 3
scenarios.situation: The growth team ran a checkout experiment, peeked on day 3, saw p<0.05 with +4% lift, and shipped it. Two weeks later, the lift has vanished and tablet conversion is down 6%.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the correct process?
choices: The experiment was too short — rerun it for exactly 30 days

Peeking without pre-commitment created a false positive; the team also failed to segment. Correct process: pre-commit duration and primary metric, no peeking, analyze once, always segment by device/traffic source before shipping
The hypothesis was wrong — pick better hypotheses
+4% was real but tablets need a separate design — ship to desktop only
scenarios.why: Two discipline failures: peeking inflates the false-positive rate (early 'significance' is often noise), and unsegmented analysis hid the tablet harm behind the average. The fix is procedural, not analytical: pre-commit the metric and duration, analyze once at the end, cut by segments before any ship decision. A shipped false positive is worse than a slow true negative — it bakes harm into the product.
scenarios.hint: What does daily peeking do to the false-positive rate? What did the average hide?
evidence: Experiment log
Day 3 peek: p=0.04, +4%. Shipped day 4. No pre-committed duration on file.
Current
Overall lift 0%; tablets -6% conversion vs control.

scenarios.title: Designing the Test
scenarios.situation: Product wants to test a new checkout flow. They propose: run it for 3 days, look at conversion, and if it's up, ship it. The checkout gets 10,000 visitors/day, baseline conversion is 5%, and they want to detect a 10% relative lift.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this plan, and what does a sound design require?
choices: Nothing — 30,000 visitors is plenty

The plan has no power analysis: at 5% baseline, detecting a 10% relative lift (5%→5.5%) needs ~60,000 visitors per arm (power 80%, α=0.05) — about 12 days, not 3. A sound design pre-registers: primary metric, MDE, sample size/duration, guardrail metrics, and the ship/no-ship rule BEFORE launch
Just run it longer until it looks significant
Test with employees first to get quick signal
scenarios.why: Three days gives ~15,000/arm — far below the ~60K needed for a 10% relative lift at 5% baseline, so the test is underpowered: a real win would likely read as noise, and noise will be mistaken for signal. Pre-registration (metric, MDE, duration, guardrails, decision rule) prevents the goalpost-moving that turns every test into a 'win'. Power analysis isn't optional rigor — it's what makes the test capable of answering the question.
scenarios.hint: How many visitors per arm does a 10% relative lift at 5% baseline actually require?
objectives: Design tests with power analysis and pre-registered decision rules
evidence: List the five elements of a pre-registered test plan

scenarios.title: The Peeking Problem
scenarios.situation: Day 4 of a 14-day test: the dashboard shows p=0.03 in favor of the variant. Product wants to ship now — 'it's significant!' You know they've checked the dashboard daily.
scenarios.prompt: How do you respond?
choices: Explain peeking: checking daily and stopping at the first p<0.05 inflates the false-positive rate far above 5% (up to 20%+ with daily peeks). Options: hold to the pre-registered duration, or use sequential testing methods (alpha spending / always-valid p-values) DESIGNED for peeking — but you can't apply them retroactively to already-peeked data
Ship it — p<0.05 is the rule
Wait one more day and check again
Average the daily p-values to be safe
scenarios.why: The 5% error rate assumes ONE look at the end. Each peek is another chance to catch a random fluctuation — daily peeking over 14 days turns α=0.05 into ~20%+ false positives. The dashboard's p-value is computed as if unpeeked, so it's invalid the moment they looked early. Sequential methods handle peeking but must be chosen upfront; retrofitting them is statistical wishful thinking.
scenarios.hint: What does the p=0.05 guarantee assume about how many times you looked?
objectives: Explain peeking inflation and enforce pre-registered durations
evidence: State the approximate false-positive rate with daily peeking over 14 days

scenarios.title: Sample Size Realities
scenarios.situation: The CEO wants to test a homepage hero change and 'get results this week'. Traffic is 2,000 visitors/day, baseline click-through 8%, and the expected lift is small (5% relative). The test has been running 5 days with no significance.
scenarios.prompt: What do you tell the CEO?
choices: Keep running — significance will come

Do the math openly: detecting a 5% relative lift at 8% baseline needs ~200,000 visitors per arm — 200 days at this traffic. The test as designed cannot answer the question this quarter. Offer the real options: test a bigger change (larger MDE), test on higher-traffic surfaces, or accept a directional read with explicit uncertainty — not a false 'result'
Lower the significance threshold to p<0.1 to get an answer faster
Stop the test and ship the new hero — design judgment beats statistics
scenarios.why: Small effects on small traffic are untestable on executive timelines — the math is the message, and hiding it produces either a false negative ('no effect' from an underpowered test) or pressure to p-hack. The honest analyst converts the constraint into options: bigger MDE (test bolder changes), more traffic (different surface), or a declared directional read. 'This week' is negotiable; the sample size isn't.
scenarios.hint: What is the required sample size — and what calendar date does that land on?
objectives: Communicate sample-size constraints to non-technical leaders
evidence: Compute the calendar duration for the required sample size

scenarios.title: Segment Surprises
scenarios.situation: Overall test result: flat, p=0.4. But slicing by platform shows mobile +12% (p=0.02) and desktop -8% (p=0.04). Product wants to ship to mobile only.
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate the segment claim?
choices: Ship to mobile — the segment result is significant
The segments cancel out, so the feature does nothing — kill it
Pick whichever segment supports shipping

Treat it as hypothesis-generating, not conclusive: with multiple segments, some will be 'significant' by chance (multiple comparisons); the interaction test (does the effect DIFFER by platform?) is the valid question, and it needs pre-registration or a replication test. Recommend: replicate mobile-only as a new pre-registered test before shipping
scenarios.why: Post-hoc slicing over k segments at α=0.05 yields false 'wins' with probability 1-(0.95)^k — with 10 segments, ~40%. The valid inference is the interaction (platform × treatment), which asks the right question directly. 'Ship to mobile' on a post-hoc slice is how companies ship noise. Replication as a pre-registered test is the honest path from surprise to decision.
scenarios.hint: If you slice by 10 segments, how many 'significant' ones do you expect by pure chance?
objectives: Handle post-hoc segments with interaction tests and replication
evidence: Compute the chance of at least one false-positive segment with 10 slices

scenarios.title: The Rollout Decision
scenarios.situation: The test won: +4% conversion, p=0.01, over the full pre-registered duration. But guardrail metrics show page load time +300ms and support tickets +6%. Product wants a full 100% rollout tomorrow.
scenarios.prompt: What is your rollout recommendation?
choices: Staged rollout with the guardrails as gates: the primary win is real, but +300ms load time compounds (and the test didn't measure long-term retention effects of slower pages). Recommend 25% → 50% → 100% with guardrail thresholds that halt the rollout, plus a holdout group to measure the load-time cost over 30 days
Full rollout — the primary metric won significantly
Don't roll out — any guardrail movement vetoes the win
Roll out to new users only, where load time matters less
scenarios.why: A significant primary metric doesn't erase guardrail regressions — +300ms on every page load is a tax on all future conversions that a 14-day test can't price. Staged rollout with halt thresholds converts the unknown into managed risk; the holdout measures what the test couldn't (long-term load-time effects). Binary ship/kill ignores the middle path that real experimentation programs use.
scenarios.hint: What did the 14-day test NOT measure that a 100% rollout would incur?
objectives: Design staged rollouts gated on guardrail metrics
evidence: Name the guardrail thresholds that would halt the rollout

scenarios.title: Interpreting the Failed Test
scenarios.situation: The test ran its full duration: -1%, p=0.6. The team calls it a failure and wants to move on. You spent 3 weeks on it. The PM says 'at least we know it doesn't work.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you extract value from the null result?
choices: Agree it's a failure and move on quickly
Rerun the test — maybe it was a fluke

Mine the null: check the confidence interval (does it rule out meaningful lifts, or was it underpowered?), examine segments for heterogeneous effects worth replicating, verify the instrumentation actually delivered the treatment (was the variant even seen?), and document the learning ('X doesn't move conversion via Y mechanism') in the experiment archive — nulls that rule things out are decisions, not failures
Tweak the variant and test again immediately
scenarios.why: A null result is information: the CI tells you whether you proved 'no meaningful effect' or just 'couldn't tell' (underpowered nulls prove nothing). The instrumentation check catches the embarrassing common case — the variant never rendered. Documented nulls prevent the team from retesting the same dead idea in 6 months. 'Failure' framing wastes the 3 weeks; learning framing banks them.
scenarios.hint: What does the confidence interval rule out — and did the variant actually reach users?
objectives: Extract decisions from null results via CIs and instrumentation checks
evidence: State what a wide vs narrow CI around zero each imply

scenarios.title: Guardrail Metrics Design
scenarios.situation: Product proposes testing a more aggressive paywall: primary metric is revenue per visitor. No guardrails are defined. You know aggressive monetization can spike refunds, hurt retention, and generate app-store review bombs.
scenarios.prompt: What guardrail set do you require before launch?
choices: No guardrails needed — revenue per visitor captures everything
Just watch revenue and cancel if it drops

Require guardrails that cover the failure modes: refund rate, 30-day retention, support ticket rate, app-store rating velocity — each with a pre-registered halt threshold. The paywall test is exactly where Goodhart's law bites: optimizing revenue/visitor without constraints optimizes FOR the failure modes
Add guardrails after the test if something looks wrong
scenarios.why: Revenue-per-visitor is maximizable by burning trust — refunds, churn, and review bombs all lag the primary metric, so the test can 'win' while destroying the business. Guardrails with halt thresholds are the circuit breakers; pre-registering them prevents the 'we'll watch it' vagueness that never actually halts anything. Monetization tests without guardrails aren't experiments, they're uncontrolled risks.
scenarios.hint: How can revenue per visitor go up while the business gets worse — list three ways.
objectives: Design guardrail metrics with halt thresholds for risky tests
evidence: Name four guardrails for a paywall test and one halt threshold

domains.name: Data Quality & Trust
domains.description: Find the lies in the data before stakeholders find them in your dashboard: validation, lineage, and the quality conversation.

scenarios.title: The Nulls That Meant Two Things
scenarios.situation: Your churn dashboard shows a spike. Digging in, you find the 'cancel_reason' column is 40% null — but some nulls mean 'customer didn't say' and others mean 'not a cancellation at all' (the ETL stamps null for non-churned rows).
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handling?
choices: Drop all nulls — incomplete data cannot be analyzed
Treat all nulls as 'unknown reason' and report the spike as-is
Separate the two populations first: filter to actually-churned rows, THEN analyze cancel reasons among them — the 40% null rate is a data-modeling artifact, not a finding
Impute the nulls with the most common reason
scenarios.why: The nulls are two different things wearing the same value: 'no reason given' vs 'not applicable'. Analyzing them together manufactures a fake spike. The fix is grain discipline: restrict to churned customers first (where cancel_reason is meaningful), then analyze. Imputation would invent data; dropping everything would discard the valid subset. Always ask what a null MEANS before deciding what to do with it.
scenarios.hint: Can a null mean two different things in one column? What question separates them?
evidence: Column profile
cancel_reason: 40% null; churned_flag: 60% of rows are non-churned (cancel_reason n/a by design)
ETL note
Pipeline writes NULL for non-churned rows; agents leave NULL when customer declines to answer.

scenarios.title: Anomaly Triage
scenarios.situation: Monday 8 AM: three alerts fire — order volume -30%, null customer emails spiking, and a schema change warning on the events table. The on-call analyst has 30 minutes before the exec standup. All three could be real or noise.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct triage order?
choices: Investigate all three in parallel — they're all alerts
Start with order volume — revenue is most important

Triage by blast radius and reversibility: schema change first (it can explain the other two — a renamed field breaks parsing, causing volume drops and nulls), then verify whether volume/nulls are downstream symptoms. One root cause beats three investigations; confirm the schema diff, then check if the other alerts resolve to it
Mute the alerts until after standup to avoid panic
scenarios.why: Correlated alerts usually share a root cause, and schema changes are the classic upstream suspect: a renamed/removed field silently breaks downstream parsing (volume drops as events fail validation; emails null as the field mapping breaks). Triaging the suspected common cause first collapses three investigations into one. Blast-radius ordering beats importance ordering when alerts may be symptoms.
scenarios.hint: What single upstream change could produce all three downstream symptoms?
objectives: Triage correlated DQ alerts by hunting common upstream causes
evidence: State the schema diff check that confirms or kills the hypothesis

scenarios.title: Root Cause: The Phantom Duplicates
scenarios.situation: The orders table has 3% duplicate order_ids this week. The dedup job runs nightly and reports success. The duplicates all share the same created_at minute, and the API team deployed a retry change on Tuesday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause chain, and the fix?
choices: Trace it: the API retry change resubmits on timeout — the first request actually succeeded (slow response, not failure), creating two orders; both land within the same minute; the dedup job keys on (order_id, created_at) or runs before the late-arriving retry lands. Fix: idempotency keys on the API (same key → same order), dedup on order_id alone, and align the dedup window with retry timing
The dedup job is broken; rewrite it
Delete the duplicates manually each week
It's only 3% — below the error budget, ignore it
scenarios.why: The evidence chain is tight: same-minute clustering + Tuesday deploy + retry change = at-least-once delivery without idempotency. The dedup 'success' is a false comfort — it dedups on the wrong key or wrong window. The real fix is at the source (idempotency keys make retries safe) plus correct dedup semantics. Manual deletion treats symptoms; the 3% compounds into revenue misstatement.
scenarios.hint: What does a client retry do when the first request succeeded but the response was slow?
objectives: Root-cause duplicates via deploy timelines and retry semantics
evidence: Name the API-side fix that makes retries safe

scenarios.title: Telling Stakeholders
scenarios.situation: You discover the conversion dashboard overstated results by 8% for 6 weeks due to a double-counting bug. The CMO presented those numbers to the board last week. The fix is deployed; historical data is corrected.
scenarios.prompt: How do you communicate this?
choices: Quietly fix it — the corrected numbers are live, no need to alarm anyone
Blame the engineer who wrote the pipeline
Wait to see if anyone notices the restated numbers

Disclose proactively with a clear structure: what was wrong (double-counting mechanism, one paragraph), the impact (8% overstatement, which decisions used it — including the board deck), what's fixed and verified, and what prevents recurrence (the new reconciliation check). Tell the CMO 1:1 BEFORE any group message so they're not blindsided twice
scenarios.why: Restated numbers WILL be noticed — by the CMO, mid-board-cycle, with no explanation. Proactive disclosure with impact scope ('which decisions used it') lets stakeholders recalibrate; the 1:1 heads-up preserves the CMO's trust and dignity. Hiding it converts a correctable error into a credibility event when (not if) it's discovered. The prevention note proves it's handled, not just patched.
scenarios.hint: Who is most harmed by learning this late — and what do they need to recalibrate?
objectives: Disclose data errors with impact scope and prevention
evidence: List the four parts of the disclosure message

scenarios.title: Designing the Monitor
scenarios.situation: After the double-counting incident, you're asked to 'add monitoring' to the conversion pipeline. The team suggests alerting on any conversion-rate change >5%. Last month had two legitimate 8% swings from campaigns.
scenarios.prompt: What monitoring design avoids alert fatigue while catching real issues?
choices: Alert on >5% changes as suggested — better safe than sorry
Alert on everything and let the on-call tune it over time
Monitoring can't catch logic bugs like double-counting, so skip it

Design layered checks: hard invariants (row counts reconcile source→mart, no null primary keys, no future timestamps) that alert immediately; statistical checks (volume/drift vs seasonal baseline with campaign calendar awareness) that alert on sustained deviation; and a daily digest for warnings. Tune thresholds on historical data to measure the false-positive rate BEFORE enabling pages
scenarios.why: A flat 5% threshold pages on every campaign — alert fatigue guarantees the real incident gets ignored. Layered design separates 'impossible' (invariants — always page) from 'unusual' (statistical — page on sustained deviation, digest the rest). Campaign-awareness prevents the known-legitimate swings from paging. Measuring the false-positive rate on history before go-live is what makes the on-call trust the alerts.
scenarios.hint: Which checks can NEVER be legitimate, vs which ones sometimes are — and should they page the same way?
objectives: Design layered DQ monitoring: invariants, statistical, digest
evidence: Name two invariant checks and one statistical check for this pipeline

scenarios.title: Negotiating the Data Contract
scenarios.situation: The mobile team ships schema changes without notice — last month a renamed field broke your funnel analysis for a week. You propose a data contract; they say 'contracts slow us down, we're agile.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you get a working contract without a turf war?
choices: Propose the minimal viable contract: only the fields you depend on are 'contracted' (name, type, nullability, semantic meaning), changes require 2 weeks notice OR a versioned parallel field, and YOU own the CI check that validates their events against the contract — framed as 'this catches your bugs before prod too', with the funnel outage as the cost of no contract
Escalate to their VP and mandate the contract
Give up — agile teams can't do contracts
Copy their events into your own pipeline so you control the schema
scenarios.why: The objection is about scope, not principle — so shrink the scope to only your depended-upon fields. The 2-week notice OR versioned-parallel-field gives them an escape hatch (agility preserved). You owning the CI check removes their work. Framing it as their bug-catcher (contract violations usually indicate THEIR bugs) aligns incentives. The outage cost makes 'slowdown' concrete: a week of broken funnels vs a 10-minute contract check.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest contract they'd accept — and what does it cost them vs the last outage?
objectives: Negotiate minimal viable data contracts with producer teams
evidence: List the four fields of a minimal data contract

scenarios.title: Incident Response
scenarios.situation: The warehouse load failed at 3 AM; the 8 AM exec dashboard will show yesterday's data as zeros. It's 7 AM. The load can be rerun (2 hours) or the dashboard can show a 'data delayed' banner with last good data.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response?
choices: Rerun the load immediately and hope it finishes by 8
Let the dashboard show zeros — it's obviously a data issue
Delay the exec meeting until the data is ready

Communicate first, then fix: post the delay notice to stakeholders NOW (before they see zeros), show last good data with a clear 'as of' banner, rerun the load, and send the all-clear with root cause later. Zeros cause wrong decisions; a banner causes a 2-hour wait — and the notice must beat the dashboard open
scenarios.why: Zeros are actionable-looking: an exec WILL make a decision on them before wondering if they're real. The banner converts a wrong-decision risk into a known wait. Communication must precede discovery — the notice at 7:15 beats the dashboard open at 8:00. The all-clear with root cause closes the loop and prevents the 'is it fixed yet?' thread. Rerunning silently gambles the 8 AM deadline on a 2-hour job.
scenarios.hint: What decision could an exec make on zeros at 8:05 — and can you unmake it at 10?
objectives: Run data incident comms: notify before discovery, banner, all-clear
evidence: Write the 7:15 AM stakeholder notice in two sentences

scenarios.title: Enforcing the Contract
scenarios.situation: You have a data contract with the mobile team, but violations keep shipping: last week a field changed type (string→int) and your pipeline cast it silently, producing garbage for 3 days before anyone noticed. The contract exists but has no teeth.
scenarios.prompt: How do you give the contract teeth?
choices: Enforce proportionally: contract validation runs in THEIR CI (fast feedback, their context), violations on contracted fields quarantine the batch (pipeline halts that feed with an alert, not silent casts — fail loudly), a weekly violation report goes to both teams' leads, and repeated violations trigger the agreed escalation (contract review meeting). Silent casts are banned: schema mismatches must fail, never coerce
Make violations block their deploy — hard gate in CI
Accept that contracts are aspirational
Add more defensive casting in your pipeline
scenarios.why: A contract without enforcement is documentation. The teeth are layered: CI validation gives fast feedback where they work; quarantine-with-alert (not silent coercion) makes violations visible instead of producing 3 days of garbage; the weekly report creates accountability without per-incident drama; the escalation path handles repeats. Banning silent casts is the key technical rule — fail loudly beats garbage quietly, always.
scenarios.hint: What turned a 1-day type change into 3 days of garbage — the change, or the silent cast?
objectives: Enforce data contracts: CI validation, quarantine, no silent coercion
evidence: State the rule for schema mismatches: fail loudly vs coerce

lessons.title: SQL for Analysis — Core concepts
concepts: Time-series analysis starts by choosing the grain: DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) buckets timestamps to month starts, then GROUP BY aggregates.

DATE_TRUNC: (Syntax varies: DATE_TRUNC in Postgres, DATETRUNC in T-SQL, DATE_FORMAT in MySQL — the concept is universal.) Also mind time zones: truncate in the business's time zone, not UTC, or month boundaries shift.
COUNT(*) counts rows (events); COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts unique users. Without truncation, every distinct timestamp is its own group — noise, not trend.

Events vs users: cohort retention: group users by signup period (the cohort), then track each cohort's activity over subsequent periods — producing retention curves. 'Active users' = distinct users; 'engagement' might = events.
Cohort curves show whether newer cohorts retain better (product improving) or all cohorts decay the same (structural problem).

lessons.title: Statistics — Core concepts
concepts: Skew: the mean is pulled by skew; the median (50th percentile) resists it.
Correlation vs causation: before acting on correlation: name plausible confounders, segment (does X help within engagement bands?), and run an experiment.
Confounders: rule: always segment by known confounders (device, source, region) before trusting an aggregate — the overall number can lie while every segment tells the truth.
A/B testing: proper A/B: randomize, pre-register the primary metric and runtime, size for statistical power (enough users to detect a meaningful effect), then read significance at the end.

lessons.title: Data Analyst — Core concepts
concepts: Aggregate with intent: SUM, COUNT, and AVG answer 'how much' and 'how many', but always check the grain first — joining before aggregating across a one-to-many relationship silently multiplies rows.
Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, SUM ... OVER) compute across rows without collapsing them — the workhorse for rankings, running totals, and period-over-period change.
Clean before you chart: strip whitespace, fix types deliberately (zip codes are text, not numbers), remove duplicates, and document every transformation so the analysis is reproducible.
Pick the chart for the question: lines for trends over time, bars for comparisons across categories — and almost never pie, because humans judge position and length far better than angle.
Summarize skew honestly: report the median alongside the mean for skewed distributions, and never average averages that were computed on different denominators.

example.code:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS m,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT m,
       revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS mom_change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY m;
example.walkthrough: The CTE first rolls orders up to one row per month, fixing the grain before any math happens. LAG then reaches back one row in month order to compute month-over-month change — no self-join needed.

pitfalls: Common trap: COUNT(column) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) counts rows — pick the one you actually mean.
Common trap: spreadsheet auto-conversion on import (leading zeros lost, dates mangled) — import IDs as text, then convert deliberately.
Common trap: a y-axis that doesn't start at zero, exaggerating tiny differences — start at zero or annotate the break.
Common trap: presenting correlation as causation in the meeting — label it 'associated with', not 'drives'.

lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Visualization flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here first, then work each domain in listed order. Domains unlock as you demonstrate mastery, because Data Analyst Interview topics build on each other.
What 'terminal' means: the Terminal tab is a real shell where labs run. Every lab command executes there — you learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Lessons teach concepts with a worked example, pitfalls, and a try-it prompt. Scenarios test judgment under realistic pressure. Labs prove you can execute. The mock assessment ties it all together.
Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts complete — you cannot click through. Spaced repetition resurfaces weak areas automatically.
Your progress syncs as you work. A domain is mastered when lessons are verified, scenarios answered, and labs completed.

example.code:
Day 1: complete all 4 Start Here lessons
Day 2-3: first two content domains (lessons + scenarios)
Day 4+: one domain per day, labs each evening
Final 3 days: mock assessment runs + capstone build
example.walkthrough: This order exists because later domains assume earlier vocabulary. Skipping ahead creates gaps that the mock assessment will expose — painfully. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skimming lessons without attempting the knowledge check — verification is the learning, not a gate to dodge.
Doing scenarios before reading the domain lessons — scenarios assume the concepts; you will guess instead of reason.
Ignoring the Terminal labs — hands-on execution is what separates passing from failing on performance-based questions.
lessons.try_it: Open the Terminal tab now and type `whoami`. That is the smallest possible lab — you just proved the environment works.

lessons.title: Data Analyst Interview Exam Strategy
concepts: Data Analyst Interview tests applied judgment more than memorization. Roughly a third of questions are scenario-based: read the situation, eliminate distractors, pick the BEST answer — not merely a correct one.
Performance-based questions (PBQs) simulate real tasks: drag-and-drop, CLI output analysis, log reading. The labs in this bootcamp are PBQ rehearsal — treat every lab as exam practice.
Time budget: divide total minutes by question count before you start, then check the clock every 20 questions. Flag hard questions and move on — a stuck minute is a lost minute.
Elimination first: cross out the two obviously wrong choices, then compare the remaining two against the question's constraints (cheapest? most secure? first step?).
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers — an educated guess beats an empty one every time.

example.code:
Q: 'A user reports... Which should you do FIRST?'
  → The word FIRST is the whole question.
  → Eliminate any choice that is a later step.
  → Among the rest, pick the diagnostic before the fix.
example.walkthrough: Exam writers love FIRST, BEST, MOST, and LEAST. Those words change the answer even when the scenario looks identical. Read the actual question stem twice — once for the story, once for the ask.

pitfalls: Answering the scenario instead of the question — the story is context; the final sentence is the task.
Changing answers on review without new evidence — first instincts outperform second-guessing statistically.
Memorizing acronyms without understanding the process behind them — PBQs punish surface knowledge.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario in this bootcamp, cover the choices, and write what the question is really asking in one sentence before looking at options.

lessons.title: Study System: Spaced Repetition That Sticks
concepts: Forgetting is the default — plan for it. Review a domain's key concepts at expanding intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Each successful recall strengthens the memory trace.
Active recall beats re-reading: close the lesson and explain the concept aloud in your own words. If you cannot explain it, you do not know it yet.
Interleave domains instead of block-studying one: mix scenarios from two domains in a session. Exams mix topics — your practice should too.
The Feynman check: after each lesson, write a 3-sentence explanation a junior could follow. Vague sentences reveal vague understanding.
Weekly rhythm: 2 domains + one analysis project per week; mock interviews at week 4 and 6.

example.code:
Session template (90 min):
  0-10   warm-up: 5 flashcards / quick recalls
  10-50  new domain: lessons + knowledge checks
  50-75  scenarios from today + one older domain (interleaving)
  75-90  one terminal lab, then 3-sentence Feynman writes
example.walkthrough: Ninety focused minutes beat four distracted hours. The template above is engineered for retention, not seat time — protect the lab block, it is where skills become reflexes.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes and calling it studying — recognition is not recall; the exam tests recall.
Cramming new domains the night before — sleep consolidates memory; an all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
Skipping the Feynman write — it feels slow, but it is the fastest diagnostic of real understanding.
lessons.try_it: Do one Feynman write right now: explain in 3 sentences what a bootcamp 'domain' is and why the order matters.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Your Unfair Advantage
concepts: Exams and interviews reward systems thinkers: people who trace a request end-to-end instead of reciting isolated facts. This bootcamp trains that explicitly in the Systems Anatomy domain.
The four-step method: (1) see the whole in context, (2) cut it open to reveal layers, (3) walk the process step-by-step, (4) pull apart into labeled pieces.
Every troubleshooting scenario here is a systems trace in disguise: start from the symptom, walk backward through dependencies, find where the expected flow diverges from reality.
In interviews, narrate the journey: 'the request starts here, then…' — hiring managers hear senior-level thinking when you trace instead of define.
The Systems Anatomy explorer in Visuals lets you step through living systems click by click. Use it before each domain's scenarios.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'DNS resolves names to IPs.'
Strong answer: 'The stub resolver asks the recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative, caching at each level — that is why the first lookup is slow and the second is instant.'
example.walkthrough: One narrated journey demonstrates more competence than ten memorized definitions. Practice this voice in every scenario's 'why' explanation — read them aloud.

pitfalls: Defining terms instead of tracing flows when asked 'how does X work?'
Jumping to fixes before mapping the system — fixes applied to the wrong layer waste time and credibility.
Treating each domain as separate — the mock assessment deliberately chains them; practice connecting domains now.
lessons.try_it: Open the Systems Anatomy domain and step through one full system in the explorer before your first study session.

lessons.title: Mock Assessment Briefing: Rules of Engagement
concepts: The mock simulates Data Analyst Interview conditions: timed, mixed-domain, no hints, one shot per question. Treat it as the real exam — same chair, same focus, no phone.
Scoring mirrors the real exam's weighting: scenario judgment counts more than recall. A wrong answer on a multi-step scenario costs more than a missed definition.
Run the mock only after all domains show 80%+ mastery. Running it early wastes its diagnostic value — it is a measuring instrument, not a study tool.
After each run, the review breaks down misses by domain. Your next study block targets exactly those domains — the mock tells you where to aim.
Two full runs minimum: the first finds gaps, the second confirms they are closed. A passing second run is your green light.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  1. Silence notifications, full-screen the bootcamp
  2. Note start time; budget per-question time on paper
  3. Answer every question — no blanks
  4. Flag-and-move on stuck questions; return with fresh eyes
  5. Review the domain breakdown before any celebration
example.walkthrough: The mock's value is the breakdown, not the score. A 68% with a clear miss-map beats a lucky 82% — the map tells you exactly what to study next.

pitfalls: Peeking at notes mid-mock — it inflates the score and destroys the diagnostic.
Running the mock as a first activity — without domain mastery it only measures unpreparedness.
Ignoring the domain breakdown — the score is trivia; the miss-map is the study plan.
lessons.try_it: Check your domain mastery percentages now. List any domain under 80% — those are your pre-mock targets.

lessons.title: Reviewing a Mock Run: Turning Misses into Mastery
concepts: For every missed question, classify the error: knowledge gap (never learned it), application gap (knew it, misapplied it), or reading error (misread the ask). Each type needs a different fix.
Knowledge gaps go back to the domain lesson — re-read, re-verify, Feynman-write. Application gaps need more scenarios, not more reading. Reading errors need the exam-strategy lesson again.
Keep an error log: question topic, error type, correct reasoning in one sentence. Patterns emerge fast — three 'reading errors' in a row is a process problem, not a knowledge problem.
Re-test missed topics within 48 hours with fresh scenarios. A corrected mistake that is not re-tested is a mistake waiting to recur.
Your second mock run should show misses migrating: fewer knowledge gaps, zero repeated reading errors. That migration is the signal you are ready.

example.code:
Error log entry:
  Q: firewall rule order scenario → chose 'deny' before 'allow'
  Type: application gap (knew rule order, misapplied under time pressure)
  Fix: 5 more firewall scenarios, timed
  Correct reasoning: 'First match wins — the allow had to precede the deny.'
example.walkthrough: Do not just re-read the explanation and move on. The error log forces you to name the failure mode — and named failures are fixable failures.

pitfalls: Re-reading explanations passively — recognition feels like learning but evaporates under pressure.
Studying only the missed topics and neglecting maintenance review of strong ones — strengths decay too.
Taking the second mock too soon — give fixes 48 hours and a re-test cycle first.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log file now (paper or notes app). You will need it after your first mock run.

lessons.title: Capstone Plan: What You Will Build and Why
concepts: Employers and examiners trust demonstrated skill over claimed knowledge. Your capstone is a working artifact — something you can screenshare and narrate in under 10 minutes.
Pick ONE project from the list below. Depth beats breadth: a single polished build outperforms three half-finished ones.
Scope it to finish in 2–3 focused sessions. If it needs more, cut features — a complete small project beats an ambitious pile of parts.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason. That log becomes your interview narration script.
Done means: it works end-to-end, you can demo it live, and you can explain every part without notes.

example.code:
Pick your project:
  1. End-to-End Analysis — a complete business analysis with dashboard and write-up
  2. Automated Reporting Pipeline — a scheduled pipeline from raw data to dashboard
  3. Experiment Analysis — a full A/B test design and analysis
example.walkthrough: Choose the project that scares you slightly — that is where the growth is. But cap the scope ruthlessly: you must finish.

pitfalls: Starting two projects and finishing neither — pick one, finish it, then consider a second.
Building without documenting — the demo narration is half the value; no log means no story.
Gold-plating instead of finishing — ship the working core first, polish only if time remains.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-paragraph project selection rationale now: which project, why it fits your goals, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Build Log: Decisions, Dead Ends, and Proof
concepts: Keep a build log with timestamps: what you tried, what happened, what you changed. Dead ends are valuable — they prove you debugged, not just followed a tutorial.
For each component, record: purpose (one line), how it works (three lines), how you tested it (one command or check).
Screenshot or record key milestones. A 60-second screen recording of the working project is worth more than a page of description.
Version your work: even a simple dated folder structure beats a single 'final' file. Show the progression.
The log is not overhead — it IS the deliverable's companion. Interviewers ask 'tell me about a challenge'; your log hands you the answer.

example.code:
Build log entry:
  14:32 — Tried X config; service failed with error Y
  14:47 — Found cause: Z was misconfigured (docs said A, reality was B)
  15:05 — Fixed; verified with [test command]; works end-to-end
example.walkthrough: Write the log as you go, not after. Memory lies; timestamps do not. Future-you (in the interview) will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Writing the log from memory at the end — you will forget the dead ends, which are the best stories.
Skipping the 'how I tested it' line — untested claims collapse under the first interview question.
No recordings — a live demo can fail; a recording is bulletproof backup.
lessons.try_it: Create your build log file now with today's date and your project title as the header.

lessons.title: Demo Day: Narrating Your Build in 10 Minutes
concepts: Structure the demo: problem (1 min) → architecture (2 min) → live walkthrough (5 min) → lessons learned (2 min). Rehearse it twice, timed.
Narrate the systems journey: 'a request starts here, flows through…' — the Systems Anatomy voice. Show you understand the whole, not just the parts you typed.
Prepare for three hard questions: 'why this approach over X?', 'what breaks at scale?', 'what would you do differently?'. Write your answers in advance.
Lead with the working demo, not slides. Working software presented live beats any deck.
End with the repo/README link and offer to walk through the code. Make it effortless for them to verify your work.

example.code:
Demo script skeleton:
  'I built [X] because [problem]. It works by [3-step journey].
   Watch: [live action]. The tricky part was [challenge] —
   I solved it by [approach]. Code and docs are at [link].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearsal is non-negotiable. A polished 10-minute demo signals preparation, communication skill, and genuine ownership — exactly what hiring managers screen for.

pitfalls: Wing the demo — 'let me just show you' without a plan wastes the moment.
Hiding the challenges — the dead ends and fixes are what prove real engineering happened.
No backup plan — have the recording ready in case live demo gods are unkind.
lessons.try_it: Draft your three hard-question answers now, before you build. They will sharpen your design decisions.

lessons.title: Roles That Hire Data Analytics Skills
concepts: The roles: Data Analyst, Business Intelligence Analyst, Analytics Engineer, Product Analyst. Read 10 job postings and extract the repeated requirements — that list is your real syllabus.
Titles vary by company; skills cluster by function. Map postings to skill clusters (not titles) to see what the market actually buys.
Entry points differ: some roles hire on certification + projects, others on portfolio + interviews. Know your target's gate before optimizing for it.
Salary bands follow scarcity + impact: specialized + revenue-adjacent pays more. Position yourself at that intersection deliberately.
Track the market quarterly: which skills are rising in postings? Your learning backlog should follow the demand signal.

example.code:
Posting analysis template:
  Role: ___
  Repeated requirements (3+ postings): ___
  Nice-to-haves: ___
  My gaps: ___ → study priority
example.walkthrough: The job posting is the employer's requirements doc. Analyze it like one — systematically, not hopefully.

pitfalls: Chasing titles instead of skill clusters — the same skills hide under five different titles.
Ignoring the 'repeated requirements' — what 8/10 postings demand is the real bar.
No gap analysis — studying without knowing your gaps is motion without direction.
lessons.try_it: Pull 5 postings for your target role now. List the top 5 repeated requirements.

lessons.title: Resume & Projects That Get Callbacks
concepts: Resumes get 30 seconds: lead with a skills line matching the posting's keywords, then 3-4 bullets per role with quantified outcomes (not duties).
Projects beat buzzwords: one deployed, documented project outweighs a paragraph of claimed skills. Link the repo AND the live demo.
Tailor per application: mirror the posting's language for the top 5 requirements. ATS filters are literal — 'PostgreSQL' does not match 'postgres' in dumb parsers.
The capstone in this bootcamp IS your resume project: finish it, document it, link it. That single line does more work than any certification bullet.
GitHub profile hygiene: pinned repos with READMEs, green contribution squares, no empty forks. Recruiters do click through.

example.code:
Bullet formula: [Action verb] + [what] + [scale] + [outcome]
  Weak: 'Responsible for databases.'
  Strong: 'Migrated 2TB analytics DB to Postgres; cut query p95 40%; zero-downtime cutover.'
example.walkthrough: Every bullet must answer: what did you do, at what scale, to what effect? Duties describe jobs; outcomes get interviews.

pitfalls: Skill lists without evidence — every claimed skill needs a project or role bullet backing it.
One generic resume for all applications — tailoring is the highest-ROI 20 minutes in job hunting.
No links — a project without a URL might as well not exist.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite your weakest resume bullet using the formula above. Quantify something.

lessons.title: Interview Loops: What Actually Happens
concepts: Typical loop: recruiter screen (15 min, fit + comp) → technical screen (45-60 min, live problems) → onsite/virtual loop (3-5 rounds: technical depth, system design, behavioral) → offer.
Technical screens test thinking aloud: narrate your approach before coding/querying. Silence is scored as stuck; structured thinking is scored as senior.
Behavioral rounds use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) — prepare 5 stories covering: conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact. Quantify results.
Questions YOU ask matter: 'what does success look like in 90 days?' and 'what's the hardest problem the team faces?' signal seriousness. Never ask nothing.
Follow up within 24 hours: thank-you note referencing something specific from the conversation. Small effort, real signal.

example.code:
STAR story skeleton:
  S: 'Our deploy pipeline broke weekly...'
  T: 'I owned stabilizing it in Q3...'
  A: 'I added staged rollouts + runbook...'
  R: 'Deploys went from 60% to 99% success; on-call pages dropped 70%.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare stories, not scripts: know your 5 STAR stories cold enough to adapt to any behavioral question. Rehearse aloud twice.

pitfalls: No questions for them — reads as disinterest; always ask two.
Rambling technical answers — structure: approach first, then detail, then verify.
Badmouthing past employers — the interviewer hears how you will talk about THEM.
lessons.try_it: Draft one STAR story now using the skeleton. Time it — aim for 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The Data Analytics Tool Landscape
concepts: Tools cluster by job-to-be-done, not by vendor. Learn the categories first, then pick one tool per category deeply — depth in one beats surface in five.
The 80/20 rule: 20% of each tool's features cover 80% of real work. Master the core workflow before exploring the edges.
Free/open tiers are enough to learn: every major platform has a free tier or community edition sufficient for portfolio projects. Never pay to learn the basics.
Tool churn is constant; fundamentals are stable. SQL outlives every BI tool; TCP/IP outlives every cloud console. Invest in fundamentals first.

For Data Analytics, the essential categories:
  SQL: Postgres/BigQuery
  BI: Power BI/Tableau
  Python: pandas
  Sheets: Excel/Google Sheets

example.code:
Learning order:
  1. One tool per category, core workflow only
  2. Build the capstone using exactly these tools
  3. Add a second tool per category only when a job posting demands it
example.walkthrough: Resist tool tourism: each new tool costs weeks. The portfolio proves depth; the resume lists breadth honestly.

pitfalls: Learning 5 tools shallowly instead of 2 deeply — interviews probe depth.
Paying for premium tiers to learn — free tiers cover 90% of learning needs.
Chasing every new release — fundamentals first; novelty second.
lessons.try_it: List your one-tool-per-category stack now. Identify any category where you have zero depth — that is your next lab.

lessons.title: Workflows: Connecting the Tools
concepts: Tools in isolation are trivia; workflows are skill. The professional unit is the end-to-end flow: ingest → transform → validate → deliver — across YOUR tool stack.
Document your workflows as runbooks: trigger, steps, verification, rollback. A runbook turns personal knowledge into team capability.
Automate the toil, not the judgment: repetitive steps get scripted; decisions stay human. If you do it weekly, automate it.
Version everything: code, configs, queries, dashboards. 'Final_v2_ACTUAL' is not version control — git is.
The workflow IS the portfolio piece: 'here is my pipeline, here is the runbook, here is the monitoring' — that sentence hires.

example.code:
Runbook skeleton:
  Trigger: ___ (schedule/event/manual)
  Steps: 1.___ 2.___ 3.___
  Verify: ___ (how do you know it worked?)
  Rollback: ___ (how do you undo it?)
  Owner: ___  Last tested: ___
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook BEFORE automating: it forces you to understand the workflow well enough to hand it to someone else.

pitfalls: Automating before documenting — you encode confusion at machine speed.
No verification step — a workflow without a check is a hope with extra steps.
No rollback plan — the first failure without one teaches this lesson permanently.
lessons.try_it: Write a runbook for one workflow you do regularly, using the skeleton above.

lessons.title: The SQL Whiteboard: Thinking Aloud
concepts: Interview SQL tests process, not syntax: narrate as you go — 'first I need the grain, so I'll start with the orders table…'. Silence reads as stuck; narration reads as senior.
Always clarify the grain first: 'one row per what?' A wrong grain assumption poisons every join after it. Ask before you write.
Build queries inside-out: start with the core table and filters, verify row counts, then add joins one at a time. Each step should be runnable mentally.
Window functions are the differentiator: ROW_NUMBER for dedup, RANK for top-N per group, LAG/LEAD for period-over-period. Practice them until they are reflex.
When stuck, say what you would check: 'I'd verify the join keys for duplicates with a GROUP BY count check.' Showing the diagnostic instinct beats a perfect query.

example.code:
-- 'Top 3 products by revenue per category, last quarter'
-- Step 1: grain = one row per product
SELECT p.category, p.product_name,
       SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-07-01'
GROUP BY p.category, p.product_name;
-- Step 2: rank within category
SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
FROM (...) t WHERE rnk <= 3;
example.walkthrough: Write the query in layers and narrate each layer's purpose. Interviewers hire the narration as much as the SQL.

pitfalls: Writing the full query silently then presenting it — no visibility into your thinking.
Skipping the grain question — the most common source of wrong-join disasters.
Reaching for DISTINCT to fix duplicate joins — it masks the grain problem instead of solving it.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario in the SQL domain and solve it aloud, narrating every decision. Record yourself once — painful, effective.

lessons.title: The Take-Home: Delivering Analysis That Gets Hired
concepts: Take-homes test judgment under ambiguity: the dataset is messy, the question is vague, and the clock is ticking. Your process documentation matters as much as the answer.
Start with data profiling before analysis: row counts, null rates, date ranges, obvious anomalies. Ten minutes of profiling prevents ten hours of wrong conclusions.
Answer the business question first, in one slide or paragraph — then show the supporting evidence. Executives read the headline; analysts who bury it fail the test.
State assumptions explicitly: 'I treated refunds as negative revenue; returns after 30 days were excluded.' Assumptions documented are assumptions defensible.
Include one 'next steps' section: what you would do with more time or data. It shows you know the analysis is never really done.

example.code:
Take-home structure:
  1. Executive summary (3 bullets: finding, implication, recommendation)
  2. Methodology + assumptions (what you did, what you assumed)
  3. Evidence (2-3 charts, each with a takeaway title)
  4. Caveats (what could be wrong)
  5. Next steps (with more time/data)
example.walkthrough: The take-home is a work sample: they are watching how you handle mess, ambiguity, and communication — not just whether the number is right.

pitfalls: Jumping to visualization before profiling — garbage in, beautiful garbage out.
Hiding assumptions — the reviewer WILL find them; disclosed assumptions are professionalism.
No caveats section — overconfident analysis reads as junior; honest limits read as senior.
lessons.try_it: Profile any dataset you have (even a CSV): row count, null %, min/max dates, top 3 anomalies. Time yourself — aim under 15 minutes.

lessons.title: Power Query: Tame Messy Data
concepts: Power Query turns the 45-minute monthly cleanup into a one-click refresh: connect, transform steps recorded, refresh when source updates. Manual cleaning is the enemy; queries are the weapon.
The applied-steps list IS your documentation: each step (remove columns, split, merge, pivot) is auditable and reorderable. Name steps clearly — future-you will thank you.
Unpivot is the most powerful move: turn wide monthly columns (Jan…Dec) into tall rows (Month, Value). Tall data pivots, charts, and analyzes; wide data fights you.
Merge queries instead of VLOOKUP across files: join on keys with explicit join types, expand only needed columns. It is a database join wearing a spreadsheet costume.
Load to the Data Model (not just a sheet) when combining tables — relationships and DAX measures beat mega-formulas for anything beyond trivial.

example.code:
Monthly sales cleanup, automated:
  1. From Folder → combine 12 CSVs
  2. Promote headers, fix types (dates as dates!)
  3. Unpivot Jan–Dec → Month, Revenue
  4. Merge with product master on SKU
  5. Load to Data Model → refresh monthly in one click
example.walkthrough: If you do it twice, query it. The second manual cleanup is the moment to open Power Query — the ROI starts immediately.

pitfalls: Cleaning in the grid instead of the query — grid edits do not refresh; query steps do.
Ignoring data types — dates-as-text break every downstream calculation silently.
VLOOKUP chains across workbooks — brittle, slow, and unauditable; merge in Power Query instead.
lessons.try_it: Take one recurring manual cleanup you do and rebuild it as a Power Query. Time both — the difference is your ROI story.

lessons.title: Designing Experiments People Can Trust
concepts: A valid experiment needs: one clear hypothesis, a primary metric decided BEFORE launch, random assignment, and a pre-committed sample size/duration. Change any mid-flight and the result is decorative.
Peeking (checking significance daily and stopping at the first green) inflates false positives dramatically. Pre-commit the runtime; analyze once at the end.
Segment your results: overall lift can hide harm. A +2% overall with -15% on mobile is not a win — it is a targeted loss wearing an average.
Practical significance beats statistical significance: a +0.1% lift with p<0.05 on massive traffic may not justify the engineering cost. Report effect size AND business impact.
Document the losers too: a well-run experiment that disproves the hypothesis is valuable — it kills a bad idea cheaply. Teams that only ship wins are not experimenting.

example.code:
Hypothesis: 'One-click checkout lifts purchase rate.'
  Primary metric: purchase conversion (decided upfront)
  Randomization: user-level, 50/50
  Duration: 14 days pre-committed (no peeking)
  Result: +1.8% overall, -3% on tablets — ship to desktop/mobile, investigate tablets
example.walkthrough: The experiment's credibility comes from its discipline, not its outcome. Pre-commitment is what separates science from storytelling.

pitfalls: Changing the primary metric after seeing results — that is called p-hacking, and reviewers spot it.
Stopping early at first significance — the false-positive rate explodes; honor the pre-committed duration.
Averaging away segment harm — always cut results by device, traffic source, and user type.
lessons.try_it: Write a one-page experiment plan for a change you'd like to test (any product). Include hypothesis, metric, randomization unit, and duration — before any data.

lessons.title: Validating Before You Visualize
concepts: Every dataset lies a little: nulls that mean 'unknown' vs 'not applicable', dates in three formats, duplicate keys, future timestamps. Profiling finds the lies before stakeholders do.

The 5-minute profile: row count, null % per column, distinct counts on keys (duplicates?), min/max on dates and numerics (outliers? future dates?), top values on categoricals (typos? 'N/A' variants?).
Lineage answers 'where did this number come from': source system → pipeline → transformation → dashboard. No lineage = no trust when the number is questioned (and it will be).
Reconcile against a second source: dashboard total vs source system total, today vs yesterday's trend. A 2% drift is a question; a 20% cliff is an incident.
When you find a quality issue, report it with impact: '3% of orders lack a region — the regional dashboard understates West by ~$40k.' Impact gets fixes; complaints get ignored.

example.code:
New 'revenue by region' dashboard:
  Profile: 3% null region, 12 duplicate order_ids, max order_date = tomorrow
  Lineage: orders → nightly ETL → warehouse → BI
  Reconcile: BI total $1.02M vs source $1.06M — 3.8% gap
  Report: 'Dashboard understates revenue ~$40k; duplicates + nulls are the cause; ETL fix proposed.'
example.walkthrough: Trust is the analyst's currency, and it is minted in validation. The analyst who catches the data lie before the meeting owns the room.

pitfalls: Assuming the warehouse is clean — warehouses store what pipelines deliver, including their bugs.
Reporting quality issues without impact framing — 'there are nulls' gets shrugged; '$40k understated' gets fixed.
Skipping reconciliation — the single cheapest trust-building habit in analytics.
lessons.try_it: Profile the next dataset you touch with the 5-minute checklist before any analysis. Note every lie you find.

lessons.title: Salary Negotiation for Analysts
concepts: Research first: levels.fyi, Glassdoor, and 3 peer conversations give you the band. Never negotiate blind — data is leverage.
The first number anchors: let them name it, or give a researched range (top of range = your target). 'Based on my research, $X–$Y is the band for this impact level.'
Negotiate the package, not just salary: signing bonus, review timeline (6-month raise clause), remote flexibility, learning budget. Total comp has more levers than base.
Use competing offers honestly: 'I have an offer at $X; I prefer you at $Y.' Never fabricate — the world is small and lies surface.
Get it in writing before signing: verbal promises evaporate. The offer letter IS the agreement; everything else is conversation.

example.code:
Script: 'I'm excited about this role. Based on the scope — owning the experimentation program — and market data, I'm looking at $X–$Y base. Is there flexibility to meet there?'
  Then SILENCE. Let them respond. The pause is the negotiation.
example.walkthrough: Negotiation is a professional skill, not a personality trait. Script it, practice it, and remember: the worst they say is no, and you still have the offer.

pitfalls: Accepting the first offer — the first number is the floor, not the ceiling.
Negotiating without data — 'I want more' loses to 'the band is $X–$Y'.
Verbal-only agreements — if it's not in the letter, it doesn't exist.
lessons.try_it: Research your target band now: 3 data points minimum. Write your range and your script.

lessons.title: Power Pivot and the Data Model
concepts: Power Pivot = real data modeling in Excel: import multiple tables, define relationships, write DAX measures. It turns Excel into a BI tool.
Relationships replace VLOOKUPs: link tables on keys once; pivot across them freely. The model IS the join logic — defined once, used everywhere.
DAX measures (see BI lesson) compute in filter context: [Total Revenue] responds to slicers automatically. Write once, slice infinitely.
Star schema applies: fact tables (transactions) + dimension tables (products, dates). Model well and the pivots practically write themselves.
When to graduate: Power Pivot handles millions of rows; beyond that (or for scheduled refresh + sharing), move to Power BI. Know the handoff point.

example.code:
Sales model:
  Tables: Orders (fact), Products (dim), Calendar (dim)
  Relationships: Orders[ProductID] → Products[ID], Orders[Date] → Calendar[Date]
  Measure: Revenue YTD = TOTALYTD(SUM(Orders[Amount]), Calendar[Date])
  Pivot: drag, slice, done — no formulas per cell.
example.walkthrough: Power Pivot is the bridge from spreadsheet analyst to BI professional. Learn the model; the tool follows.

pitfalls: Flattened mega-tables — defeats the model; normalize into facts and dimensions.
Calculated columns for everything — measures compute dynamically; columns bloat.
No relationships defined — then it's just separate tables; the model needs the links.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a 3-table data model for data you work with. Define the relationships and one measure.

lessons.title: Bayesian A/B Testing Intro
concepts: Frequentist asks 'is it significant?'; Bayesian asks 'what's the probability B beats A?' — the business question, directly answered. P(B>A | data) is the deliverable.
Priors matter but wash out: start with uninformative priors (Beta(1,1)); with enough data, the data dominates. Document the prior — transparency, not trickery.
The output is a distribution, not a verdict: 'B beats A by 1-3% with 92% probability.' Decisions use expected loss: ship if P(loss) is acceptably small.
Peeking is less sinful (but not innocent): Bayesian updating is coherent under optional stopping, but the decision rule still needs pre-commitment to avoid bias.
Tools: simple Beta-Binomial for conversion rates (conjugate, closed-form); MCMC (PyMC) for complex models. Start simple — most tests need only Beta-Binomial.

example.code:
Beta-Binomial:
  Prior: Beta(1,1) for both variants
  Data: A: 120/1000, B: 150/1000
  Posterior: A ~ Beta(121, 881), B ~ Beta(151, 851)
  P(B>A) = 0.93 via sampling. Expected loss of shipping B: tiny.
  Decision: ship B. The probability IS the justification.
example.walkthrough: Bayesian testing answers the question stakeholders actually ask. Learn Beta-Binomial deeply; it covers 80% of conversion tests.

pitfalls: Priors as weapons — strong priors need justification; default to weak and let data speak.
Ignoring the loss function — probability without cost is half a decision; add expected loss.
MCMC for simple problems — conjugate models are exact and instant; save MCMC for hierarchies.
lessons.try_it: Compute P(B>A) for the example above via simulation (10k draws). Verify ~0.93.

lessons.title: Building a Data Quality Dashboard
concepts: The DQ dashboard monitors: freshness (is data late?), volume (row counts vs expected), validity (null rates, range violations), and consistency (cross-source reconciliation). Four panels, full coverage.
Thresholds with history: alert when today's metric deviates from the 30-day baseline — not on fixed magic numbers. Baselines adapt; fixed thresholds rot.
Each alert links to the runbook: 'null rate spike → check upstream job X, contact Y'. Alerts without runbooks are anxiety; with runbooks, they're routine.
Trend the metrics: null-rate over time, freshness drift, reconciliation gaps. Trends show decay before incidents — the dashboard is early warning, not autopsy.
Review cadence: weekly 15-minute DQ review with pipeline owners. The dashboard drives the conversation; ownership drives the fixes.

example.code:
DQ dashboard panels:
  1. Freshness: max(event_time) vs now — per pipeline
  2. Volume: today's rows vs 30-day band
  3. Validity: null %, range violations — top 5 tables
  4. Reconciliation: BI total vs source total — the trust number
  Alert: any panel red → runbook link attached.
example.walkthrough: A DQ dashboard turns data quality from complaints into operations. Build it for your top 5 tables first — expand from proven value.

pitfalls: Alerting without runbooks — every alert must link to the fix procedure.
Fixed thresholds — baselines adapt; magic numbers don't.
Dashboard nobody reviews — the weekly 15-minute review is the actual control.
lessons.try_it: Sketch the 4-panel DQ dashboard for your data. What are today's values? Any red?

lessons.title: CTEs: Queries You Can Read
concepts: CTEs (WITH clauses) turn nested subqueries into named, readable steps: each CTE is a labeled intermediate result. Read top-to-bottom instead of inside-out.
Use CTEs for: multi-step aggregations (aggregate, then filter the aggregates), self-joins (employees and managers), and recursion (org charts, BOM explosions).
CTEs are optimization fences in Postgres (materialized by default until v12) — fine for readability; for performance-critical paths, test against temp tables.
Name CTEs as business concepts (monthly_revenue, churned_users), not t1/t2. The name IS the documentation — future readers thank you.

example.walkthrough: Write queries as stories: WITH sets the scene, each CTE is a chapter, the final SELECT is the moral. Readable queries get maintained; clever ones get rewritten.

pitfalls: Nesting 5 subqueries deep — the next person (you, in 3 months) cannot read it; CTE it.
CTE names like t1, x, temp — the name should say what the data MEANS.
Assuming CTEs are free — in some engines they materialize; check the plan on big data.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite your most-nested subquery as CTEs. Compare readability honestly.

lessons.title: Date Math Without Tears
concepts: Date truncation is the analyst's bread: date_trunc('month', ts) buckets timestamps. Know your engine's function (DATE_TRUNC, DATE_FORMAT, strftime) — they differ, the concept doesn't.
Intervals done right: ts + INTERVAL '30 days' (Postgres), DATE_ADD(ts, INTERVAL 30 DAY) (MySQL). Never do string math on dates — the type system is your friend.
Timezones will burn you: store UTC, convert at presentation. AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York' (Postgres) — and know that DST makes some local times ambiguous.
Date spines: generate_series fills gaps (days with zero orders still appear). Missing rows are invisible in GROUP BY — the spine makes absence visible.

example.code:
-- Daily revenue with zero-filled gaps (Postgres):
WITH spine AS (
  SELECT generate_series('2026-01-01'::date, '2026-01-31', '1 day') AS d
)
SELECT s.d, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM spine s LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date::date = s.d
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
example.walkthrough: Dates are the most lied-about type in analytics: timezones, gaps, and string math. Master the type and half your 'data quality issues' vanish.

pitfalls: String manipulation on dates — SUBSTRING(order_date, 1, 7) is a bug factory; use date_trunc.
Ignoring timezones — 'midnight' in whose timezone? Store UTC, convert late.
Missing the gaps — zero-order days vanish in GROUP BY; the spine reveals them.
lessons.try_it: Write a month-over-month growth query for any date column you know, with zero-filled gaps.

lessons.title: INDEX/MATCH: VLOOKUP's Grown-Up Sibling
concepts: VLOOKUP breaks when columns move (hardcoded index) and only looks right. INDEX/MATCH looks both directions and survives column inserts — the professional choice.
Pattern: =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0)). MATCH finds the row; INDEX fetches from it. Two functions, one robust lookup.
