XLOOKUP (modern Excel) combines both with built-in if-not-found: =XLOOKUP(value, lookup_range, return_range, "missing"). Use it where available; know INDEX/MATCH for legacy files.
Match type matters: 0 = exact (almost always what you want), 1/-1 = approximate (sorted data only). Wrong match type = silently wrong answers.

example.code:
=INDEX(Products[Price], MATCH([@SKU], Products[SKU], 0))
  Structured references (Tables): self-documenting, auto-expanding.
  vs =VLOOKUP([@SKU], Products!A:D, 4, FALSE) — breaks if a column is inserted.
example.walkthrough: Graduate from VLOOKUP: the 10 minutes learning INDEX/MATCH pays back every week in robustness. Tables + XLOOKUP is the modern endgame.

pitfalls: VLOOKUP with hardcoded column index — one inserted column, all wrong, silently.
Approximate match on unsorted data — garbage results that look plausible.
Full-column references on big data — the spinning wheel of death; bound ranges or use Tables.
lessons.try_it: Convert one VLOOKUP you use into INDEX/MATCH (or XLOOKUP). Test with a column inserted — watch it survive.

lessons.title: PivotTables: The 80/20 Analysis Tool
concepts: Drag-drop analysis: rows (categories), values (aggregations), filters (slicers). A pivot answers 'revenue by region by quarter' in 30 seconds — the fastest BI in existence.
Value field settings matter: SUM vs COUNT vs AVERAGE answer different questions. 'Average of averages' trap: pivot averages of pre-averaged data without weighting.
Grouping: dates group by month/quarter/year (right-click → Group); numbers group into bins. Grouping turns raw lists into distributions.
Slicers + timelines make pivots interactive dashboards: click a region, everything filters. Share the workbook, not screenshots — let stakeholders explore.

example.code:
Monthly churn pivot:
  Rows: Cancel Month (grouped by quarter)
  Columns: Plan Tier
  Values: Count of Customer ID, Avg of Tenure
  Slicer: Region
  Insight in 60 seconds: which tier/quarter bleeds? The pivot shows it.
example.walkthrough: Before building a dashboard, pivot the data: 80% of ad-hoc questions die at the pivot stage. Dashboards are for the recurring 20%.

pitfalls: Stale pivot cache — Refresh All is part of the workflow, not optional.
Average of averages — weight by the underlying counts or recompute from base data.
Screenshot sharing — share the workbook; stakeholders ask follow-ups the screenshot cannot answer.
lessons.try_it: Build a pivot on real data now: one categorical row, one date grouping, two value fields. Add a slicer.

lessons.title: Data Validation: Spreadsheets That Refuse Bad Data
concepts: Data Validation rules prevent bad entry: dropdown lists (categories), whole numbers in range, dates between bounds, custom formulas. Prevention beats cleanup 100:1.
Dropdowns from named ranges: define the list once (Products_Categories), reference everywhere. One source of truth — change the range, update everywhere.
Custom formula validation is the power tool: =COUNTIF($A:$A, A1)=1 enforces uniqueness; =ISNUMBER(SEARCH("@",A1)) demands an email shape. Logic as validation.
Protect the structure: sheet protection (locked formula cells, unlocked input cells) + workbook protection. Users fill inputs; formulas are untouchable.

example.code:
Order entry sheet:
  Category: dropdown from Categories range (Stop on invalid)
  Quantity: whole number 1-1000
  Email: custom =ISNUMBER(SEARCH("@",A1))
  SKU: custom =COUNTIF($B:$B,B1)=1 (unique)
  Formulas locked; inputs open. Bad data cannot enter.
example.walkthrough: The best spreadsheet is one where errors are impossible, not just detectable. Validation at entry is the cheapest data quality investment.

pitfalls: No validation on shared sheets — 10 editors, 10 formats, one mess.
Free-text categories — 'NYC', 'New York', 'nyc' are three categories to a pivot; dropdowns fix it.
Unlocked formula cells — one accidental overwrite, silent wrongness everywhere.
lessons.try_it: Add validation to one shared sheet you own: one dropdown, one numeric range, one custom rule.

lessons.title: Chart Selection: The Right Picture
concepts: Match chart to question: comparison → bar; trend over time → line; part-of-whole → stacked bar (rarely pie); distribution → histogram; relationship → scatter.
Pie charts are almost always wrong: humans compare angles poorly. Two slices OK; five slices are decoration. Bar charts beat pies in every serious comparison.
Dual axes mislead: two scales invite false correlation readings. Facet (small multiples) or indexed lines instead — honest comparisons share a scale.
Start axes at zero for bar/column (length encodes value); line charts may truncate ONLY with clear labeling. Truncated bars lie visually.
One chart, one message: the title states the takeaway ('Churn concentrated in Q1 signups'), not the description ('Churn by quarter'). Titles argue; labels describe.

example.code:
Wrong: pie with 8 slices titled 'Revenue breakdown'
  Right: horizontal bar, sorted desc, titled
    'Enterprise = 58% of revenue — concentration risk'
  Same data, honest picture, actionable title.
example.walkthrough: The chart is an argument, not decoration. If you cannot state its message in one sentence, the chart is not ready.

pitfalls: Pie charts with many slices — unreadable; use sorted bars.
Dual axes without labeling — manufactured correlations; facet instead.
Truncated bar axes — visual lies; start at zero or use lines.
lessons.try_it: Take your last chart. Rewrite its title as the takeaway message. Does the chart type support it?

lessons.title: Dashboards Stakeholders Actually Use
concepts: Design for the decision: what will the viewer DO with this dashboard? Every element must serve a decision — decoration gets cut.
The 5-second rule: the top KPI row answers 'how are we doing' in 5 seconds. Details live below the fold for those who want them.
Hierarchy: KPIs → trends → breakdowns → raw tables. The eye travels top-left to bottom-right; put conclusions where eyes land first.
Interactivity with purpose: filters for the dimensions stakeholders actually slice (region, segment, time). Ten filters = no filters; curate to 3-4.
Performance is a feature: dashboards that load in 30 seconds get opened once. Aggregate, cache, limit date ranges — speed is respect for the user's time.

example.code:
Executive dashboard:
  Row 1: Revenue MTD | vs target | Churn % (3 big numbers)
  Row 2: Revenue trend (12 mo line) + churn trend
  Row 3: Breakdown by segment (bar) with region filter
  Row 4: Top 10 at-risk accounts (table, drill-through)
  Decision served: where to focus retention effort.
example.walkthrough: A dashboard is a product with users. Interview 3 stakeholders before building: 'what decision does this inform?' Build for the answer.

pitfalls: Vanity metrics — totals without context or actionability.
Cluttered everything-on-one-page — hierarchy exists; use it.
No refresh expectations set — 'as of' timestamps prevent stale-data arguments.
lessons.try_it: Sketch your next dashboard on paper first: KPI row, then trends, then breakdowns. Show it to one stakeholder before building.

lessons.title: Color and Accessibility in Charts
concepts: Color encodes, not decorates: one hue for categories (colorblind-safe palette), intensity for magnitude, red/green ONLY with labels (8% of men are red-green colorblind).
Test in grayscale: print or desaturate — if the chart is unreadable, color was carrying meaning it should not carry alone. Labels and position must work without color.
Highlight, don't rainbow: gray everything, color the ONE thing that matters (the insight). The eye goes to color — spend it on the message.
Consistent semantics: the same blue = the same entity across all charts in a deck. Changing colors per slide forces relearning — respect the viewer's memory.
Alt text and data tables: screen readers need the message in words. Every published chart gets a 1-sentence alt text stating the takeaway.

example.code:
Before: 8-category rainbow pie, red/green for good/bad, no labels.
  After: sorted gray bars, ONE blue bar for 'our segment',
    direct labels on bars, title states the insight.
  Same data; the second version is readable by everyone.
example.walkthrough: Accessible charts are better charts for everyone: the constraints (label directly, highlight sparingly) improve clarity universally.

pitfalls: Red/green without labels — invisible to the colorblind; always pair with text or position.
Rainbow palettes — visual noise; one highlight color + grays.
No alt text on published charts — excluding screen-reader users is a choice; choose inclusion.
lessons.try_it: Take one of your charts: desaturate it. Can you still read the message? Fix what breaks.

lessons.title: Descriptive Stats That Don't Lie
concepts: Report the five-number summary (min, Q1, median, Q3, max) before any mean: it reveals skew, outliers, and spread that a single average hides.
Mean vs median is a skew detector: mean >> median means right skew (a few huge values). Report both; lead with the median for skewed data.
Standard deviation needs context: SD of 10 on a mean of 1000 is tight; on a mean of 15 it is wild. Coefficient of variation (SD/mean) compares spread across scales.
Outliers: investigate before deleting. A $1M 'order' might be the enterprise deal of the quarter or a data entry error — the business context decides, not the z-score.
Sample size qualifies everything: a 5% difference on n=30 is noise; on n=30,000 it is signal. Always report n alongside any statistic.

example.code:
Order values: mean $240, median $45, max $180,000.
  Honest report: 'Typical order $45 (median); mean inflated by 3 enterprise deals; excluding top 1%, mean $52.'
  One paragraph, no lies, all context.
example.walkthrough: Descriptive statistics are the analyst's oath: describe the data as it is, with its skew and warts — not as the average pretends it to be.

pitfalls: Mean-only reporting on skewed data — the classic $240 'average order' lie.
Deleting outliers silently — investigate first; document the decision always.
No sample sizes — a percentage without n is a rumor.
lessons.try_it: Take any metric you report. Compute the five-number summary. Does your usual headline survive?

lessons.title: Correlation in Practice
concepts: Pearson measures linear co-movement (-1 to 1); Spearman measures monotonic rank co-movement (robust to outliers and curves). Choose by the relationship shape, not habit.
Always plot first: Anscombe's quartet proves identical correlations (0.816) can hide wildly different relationships — including a dinosaur. The scatterplot is mandatory.
Confounders to hunt: time trends (both rising?), selection effects, and size (bigger things have more of everything). Stratify or regress before claiming.
For feature selection: correlation with target is a start, but check multicollinearity among features (VIF) — redundant features add noise, not signal.
Report with uncertainty: r=0.6, n=50 has a wide confidence interval. Small-n correlations are suggestions, not findings.

example.code:
Ad spend vs revenue: r=0.85 — exciting!
  Plot: both rise over time (trend confound).
  Detrended (month-over-month changes): r=0.2 — the 'relationship' was shared growth.
  The plot + detrending saved a bad budget decision.
example.walkthrough: Correlation is the start of an investigation, not its conclusion. Plot, deconfound, then — maybe — believe.

pitfalls: Pearson on nonlinear relationships — a U-shape scores ~0; the plot would have shown it.
Ignoring confounders — time is the usual suspect; always check.
Causal language from correlation — 'linked to' is honest; 'drives' needs an experiment.
lessons.try_it: Find two correlated metrics you track. Plot them, then check for a time confound. What survives?

lessons.title: Sampling: Getting It Right
concepts: Random sampling is the foundation: every member has a known, non-zero chance. Convenience samples ('surveyed our Twitter followers') generalize to nobody.
Stratified sampling guarantees subgroup representation: sample proportionally from each segment (region, tier). Essential when subgroups behave differently.
Sample size math: n depends on desired margin of error and confidence, NOT population size (beyond small populations). A 1,000-person survey works for 10k or 10M people.
Non-response bias is the silent killer: 10% response rate means the 90% who ignored you might differ systematically. Weight or acknowledge — never ignore.
For A/B tests: randomize at the right unit (user, not session, usually), pre-commit sample size, and check for sample ratio mismatch (SRM) — unequal splits signal broken randomization.

example.code:
Survey: 2,000 responses, 8% response rate, all from power users.
  Honest report: 'Findings represent engaged users only; non-users (the churn risk!) are unrepresented.'
  Fix next time: stratified outreach + incentives for dormant segments.
  The caveat IS the professionalism.
example.walkthrough: Every analysis generalizes from a sample to a population. Name your sampling method and its limits — or your conclusions overclaim.

pitfalls: Convenience samples presented as representative — the most common sampling sin.
Ignoring non-response — the missing 90% are data about your data.
No SRM check in experiments — broken randomization poisons everything downstream.
lessons.try_it: Describe the sampling behind your last analysis. Who was excluded? State the limits in two sentences.

lessons.title: Data Modeling for BI
concepts: Star schemas win for BI: fact tables (events, transactions — narrow, long) joined to dimension tables (customers, products — wide, descriptive). Simple, fast, understandable.
Grain discipline: one row per WHAT in each fact table? Declare it, document it, defend it. Grain confusion is the #1 BI bug — every wrong total traces back here.
Dimensions are conformed (shared across facts): one customer dimension, not three copies. Conformed dimensions make cross-fact analysis possible.
Slowly changing dimensions: Type 1 (overwrite — history lost), Type 2 (new row per change — history kept). Customer address changes: Type 2 if history matters for analysis.
The semantic layer (metrics definitions) is the real product: 'revenue' defined once, used everywhere. Ten definitions of revenue = ten arguments in every meeting.

example.code:
Orders star:
  fact_orders: one row per order line (grain!)
    keys: order_id, customer_key, product_key, date_key
    measures: quantity, unit_price, discount
  dim_customer: customer_key, name, segment, region (SCD2)
  dim_date: date_key, month, quarter, is_weekend
  Every BI question starts here — the model IS the analysis foundation.
example.walkthrough: Model before you visualize: an hour on the star schema saves ten hours of dashboard debugging. The model is the thinking; the dashboard is the typing.

pitfalls: Fact tables at mixed grains — order headers and lines in one table; totals double-count.
Ten definitions of revenue — the semantic layer exists to end this war.
No SCD strategy — 'why did last quarter's numbers change?' has no answer without history.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a star schema for a business you know: one fact, three dimensions, declared grain. Defend the grain choice.

lessons.title: DAX / Measure Fundamentals
concepts: Measures calculate in filter context: SUM(Sales[Amount]) respects the slicers. Calculated columns compute row-by-row at refresh. Mixing them up is the #1 DAX confusion.
Filter context vs row context: measures respond to filters (slicers, rows); calculated columns see only their row. 90% of 'wrong DAX' is context confusion.
CALCULATE is the superpower: CALCULATE(SUM(...), FILTER(...)) modifies filter context — time intelligence (SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR), selective filters, all live here.
Time intelligence needs a proper date table: continuous dates, marked as date table. Without it, YTD/MTD measures silently misbehave.
Performance: measures compute on the fly (fast on aggregated models); calculated columns bloat the model. Prefer measures; use columns only for slicers/axes.

example.code:
-- YTD Revenue (needs date table):
YTD Revenue = TOTALYTD(SUM(Sales[Amount]), 'Date'[Date])
-- vs prior year:
YoY Growth = DIVIDE([Revenue] - [Revenue LY], [Revenue LY])
-- The pattern: base measure → time-intelligence variants.
example.walkthrough: Think in filter context: 'what filters are active on this cell?' Answer that, and DAX becomes predictable instead of magical.

pitfalls: Calculated columns for aggregations — bloats the model; measures compute dynamically.
No date table — time intelligence without one is a bug farm.
Hardcoded filters in every measure — use variables and base measures; DRY applies to DAX.
lessons.try_it: Write three measures: base revenue, YTD revenue, YoY growth. Identify the filter context each responds to.

lessons.title: BI Performance Tuning
concepts: The 10-second rule: dashboards must feel instant. Over 10 seconds, usage dies. Performance is adoption.
Aggregate tables: pre-compute common grains (daily, monthly). The dashboard queries 365 rows, not 365M — the oldest trick and still the best.
Import vs DirectQuery: import (fast, scheduled refresh) for most; DirectQuery (live, slower) only when real-time is truly required. Hybrid: aggregate in import, detail in DQ.
Reduce what loads: remove unused columns/tables, set proper data types, avoid bi-directional relationships (they confuse the engine and the user).
Measure with Performance Analyzer: find the slow visual, see its DAX query, optimize THAT. Tuning without measurement is guessing.

example.code:
Slow dashboard autopsy:
  Performance Analyzer: one matrix visual = 8s (of 12s total).
  Cause: 50k-row detail at transaction grain + 12 measures.
  Fix: aggregate to daily (365 rows) + drill-through for detail.
  Result: 1.2s. The detail is one click away, not on the main page.
example.walkthrough: Performance tuning is user-experience work: every second of load time costs engagement. Measure, aggregate, verify.

pitfalls: DirectQuery for everything — live data at glacial speed; import unless real-time is proven necessary.
Transaction-grain dashboards — aggregate first, drill second.
No measurement — 'feels slow' is not a diagnosis; Performance Analyzer is.
lessons.try_it: Run Performance Analyzer on your slowest dashboard. What is the single slowest visual? Why?

lessons.title: The 3-Minute Data Story
concepts: Structure: Hook (the surprising finding) → Context (why it matters) → Evidence (2-3 charts) → Recommendation (what to do) → Caveats (what could be wrong). Five parts, three minutes.
Lead with the insight, not the methodology: 'Churn is concentrated in first-month mobile users' beats 'I analyzed 2M rows using...'. Method belongs in the appendix.
One story per presentation: three findings = three stories = confusion. Pick the most important, tell it well, mention others as 'also worth noting'.
The recommendation needs an owner and a next step: 'Marketing should test onboarding emails for mobile signups starting next sprint.' Insight without action is trivia.
End with the caveat: 'This assumes X; if Y, the conclusion changes.' Honest limits build trust; false certainty destroys it when reality disagrees.

example.code:
3-minute story:
  Hook: '40% of churn happens in week 1 — on mobile only.'
  Context: 'Mobile is 70% of signups; week-1 experience decides.'
  Evidence: [churn curve by platform] [onboarding funnel]
  Ask: 'Test a mobile onboarding checklist next sprint.'
  Caveat: 'iOS 17 changed tracking; Android may differ.'
example.walkthrough: Data storytelling is translation: from analysis to decision. The story is done when the stakeholder knows what to DO.

pitfalls: Methodology-first presentations — the audience tunes out before the insight.
Three stories in one deck — pick the winner; mention the rest.
No recommendation — 'interesting' is not actionable; always propose the next step.
lessons.try_it: Take your last analysis. Write the 5-part story in under 200 words. Time a 3-minute delivery.

lessons.title: Visualizations That Persuade
concepts: Persuasion needs emphasis: gray everything, color the insight. The audience's eye goes to color — spend it on the conclusion.
Annotate directly on the chart: arrows, callouts, reference lines. 'Churn spike: pricing change launched' ON the chart beats a paragraph beside it.
Progressive reveal: build the story slide by slide — baseline first, then the anomaly, then the cause. Each slide earns the next.
Kill the chartjunk: 3D effects, gradients, decorative icons — all noise. Data-ink ratio: maximize ink that encodes data, minimize the rest.
The takeaway title: every chart gets a title that states the conclusion ('Mobile churn 3x desktop'), not the description ('Churn by platform').

example.code:
Before: default Excel chart, rainbow colors, title 'Q3 Metrics'.
  After: gray bars, ONE blue bar (the insight), direct labels,
    annotation arrow ('pricing change'), title:
    'Q3 churn spike driven entirely by mobile (pricing change)'.
  Same data; the second one persuades.
example.walkthrough: A persuasive chart does the thinking FOR the viewer: the conclusion is visible before the details are examined. Design for the 5-second glance.

pitfalls: Rainbow charts with legend-hunting — direct labels beat legends always.
Description titles — titles argue; 'Q3 metrics' argues nothing.
Unexplained anomalies — annotate the spike or the audience invents explanations.
lessons.try_it: Redesign your most important chart: gray + one highlight, direct labels, takeaway title, one annotation.

lessons.title: Handling Hostile Questions
concepts: Anticipate the attacks: 'Is the data reliable?' (show validation), 'What about X segment?' (have the cut ready), 'Correlation isn't causation' (agree + show the experiment plan).
The 3-part defense: acknowledge ('good question'), answer with evidence ('the segment cut shows...'), bridge back ('which is why we recommend...'). Never defensive, always substantive.
'I don't know' is allowed — followed by 'here's how I'd find out by Friday.' Bluffing destroys credibility permanently; honesty + plan builds it.
Bring the appendix: 5 backup slides with the cuts, caveats, and methods. 'I have that cut right here' defuses 80% of challenges instantly.
Separate the person from the question: the hostile questioner is often testing rigor, not attacking you. Answer the question, not the tone.

example.code:
Attack: 'Your churn analysis ignores seasonality!'
  Defense: 'Good catch — we checked: [backup slide] churn by cohort shows
    the spike persists after seasonal adjustment. The appendix has
    the full decomposition. The recommendation stands, and we will
    monitor seasonally going forward.'
example.walkthrough: Hostile questions are free consulting: they reveal what your analysis must defend. Prepare the defenses before the meeting, not during.

pitfalls: Bluffing through — one caught bluff ends your credibility for the whole meeting.
No appendix — 'I'll get back to you' on a predictable question looks unprepared.
Taking it personally — answer the content; the tone is their problem.
lessons.try_it: List the 5 most likely attacks on your current analysis. Prepare the one-slide defense for each.

lessons.title: Window Functions in Practice
concepts: Window functions compute across rows without collapsing them: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, and running SUM/AVG all add a computed column while keeping every row — the key difference from GROUP BY, which destroys row-level detail.

PARTITION BY defines the 'window' (per user, per month, per region); ORDER BY inside the OVER clause defines the sequence the function walks. Getting these two clauses right is 90% of window-function mastery.

LAG/LEAD turn time-series questions into row comparisons: month-over-month change is (value - LAG(value)) / LAG(value) — no self-join needed. The gaps-and-islands trick (date minus row_number is constant within a consecutive run) solves 'N months in a row' elegantly.
Frame clauses (ROWS BETWEEN) control running totals precisely: the default frame can surprise you with peer rows (RANGE vs ROWS), so specify the frame explicitly for running calculations.

example.code:
-- month-over-month growth per region, no self-join
SELECT region, month, revenue,
  revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month)
    AS mom_change,
  AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_3mo
FROM monthly_revenue;
example.walkthrough: LAG reaches back one row within each region's time order — the month-over-month change falls out with no join. The rolling average uses an explicit ROWS frame so it's exactly 3 months, not '3 months plus peers.' Window functions keep every row, so you can filter, sort, and drill into the same result set.

pitfalls: Forgetting PARTITION BY and computing the window over the whole table — every region's numbers bleed together.
Relying on the default frame with ORDER BY on non-unique values — peer rows silently join the frame (RANGE behavior).
Using window functions where GROUP BY belongs, then DISTINCT-ing away the duplicated rows you created.
lessons.try_it: On a monthly revenue table, compute MoM change, rolling 3-month average, and each month's rank within its year — all in one query, no self-joins.

lessons.title: Choosing Chart Types That Answer Questions
concepts: Choose the chart by the question: trend over time → line; comparison across categories → bar; part-to-whole → stacked bar (not pie, beyond 2–3 slices); distribution → histogram; relationship → scatter. The question dictates the geometry.

Lines imply continuity — never use a line chart for categorical data (it fabricates a trend between unrelated categories). Bars imply discrete comparison — never use bars for continuous time at fine granularity.

Dual axes are guilty until proven innocent: they let you scale two series to imply any correlation. Prefer indexed series (both rebased to 100) or small multiples when comparing series of different magnitudes.
Every chart needs a takeaway title (the conclusion, not 'Revenue by Month'), labeled axes with units, and the anomaly annotated ON the chart. A chart without a conclusion is a Rorschach test.

example.code:
-- the decision in pseudocode:
-- Q: 'Is churn trending up?'        -> line, y from 0, annotate the backfill
-- Q: 'Which segment churns most?'   -> sorted bar, one highlight color
-- Q: 'Where do orders cluster?'     -> histogram, not an average in a KPI card
-- title = the answer: 'Churn flat at 4.5% after March backfill'
example.walkthrough: Write the question first, then pick the geometry that answers it — trend, comparison, composition, or distribution. Title the chart with the answer, not the topic. Annotate the anomaly where it happened so the context travels with the image when it's screenshotted into Slack.

pitfalls: Pie charts with 7 slices — the eye can't compare angles; use a sorted bar.
Truncated y-axes that turn noise into drama (the #1 executive-misleading chart).
3D effects, which distort the very proportions the chart exists to show.
lessons.try_it: Take one dashboard chart and rewrite it: question-first, correct geometry, takeaway title, annotated anomaly. Show the before/after to a colleague and time their comprehension.

lessons.title: Walking Through a Case Study
concepts: The case interview scores structure, not speed: clarify the metric (conversion of WHAT over WHAT), segment before explaining (cohort? platform? geography?), and enumerate hypotheses INCLUDING data-quality ones (tracking breaks cause 'drops' constantly).
State your plan before executing: 'First I'll check the trend by segment to localize, then test the top two hypotheses...' Interviewers score the plan; the query is just evidence you can execute it.
Narrate trade-offs as you go: 'This cut answers X but conflates Y, so I'll follow with...' — showing you see the limits of each analysis is senior signal.
Close with a recommendation AND next steps: the decision the business should make plus what you'd validate with another day. Cases that end in analysis without a decision feel unfinished.

example.code:
Case: 'Conversion dropped 20% last quarter.'
1. Scope: 'Conversion = paid / trial-started? Over which window?'
2. Segment: by cohort, platform, plan tier -> localize the drop
3. Hypotheses: mix shift, product change, pricing change, tracking break, seasonality
4. Test order: cheapest disproof first (tracking, seasonality)
5. Recommend + next validation step
example.walkthrough: Open by scoping the metric — half of 'drops' are definition changes. Segment to localize: a 20% drop in one cohort is a different case than a broad decline. List hypotheses out loud including the boring data-quality ones, then propose the test order. The interviewer is grading your thinking sequence, not your SQL.

pitfalls: Querying immediately — busy hands, unstructured head.
Forgetting data-quality hypotheses; every experienced interviewer includes a tracking-break trap.
Ending with 'interesting findings' instead of a recommendation the business can act on.
lessons.try_it: Take any metric drop and do a 5-minute spoken walkthrough: scope, segment plan, hypothesis list, test order, recommendation. Record yourself and check you stated the plan before any 'querying.'

lessons.title: Power Query Fundamentals
concepts: Power Query is a recorded transformation pipeline: every click becomes an M step in the Applied Steps list. Next month's file runs the same steps via Refresh — the transformation is documentation, not tribal knowledge.

The core operations cover 90% of cleaning: split columns, change type (explicitly — Power Query's auto-types are a trap), filter rows, remove duplicates, merge queries (joins), group by (aggregations), unpivot (wide-to-long).

Set types explicitly as the FIRST step after load: Power Query guesses types from the first rows, and a text value in row 50,000 becomes an error. Explicit type-setting is the difference between a robust query and a monthly mystery.
Merge (join) in Power Query beats VLOOKUP chains: it's a proper join with match diagnostics (how many rows matched?), it doesn't depend on column positions, and the logic is visible in the steps.

example.walkthrough: Load the CSV, promote headers, then immediately set every column's type explicitly — this is the step everyone skips and regrets. Split, merge, and group through the UI, watching each Applied Step appear. Save; next month is one Refresh click instead of a rebuild. Check the merge's match percentage — unmatched rows are your data-quality signal.

pitfalls: Trusting auto-detected types — one text value deep in the file breaks the whole column.
Hardcoding the file path so Refresh breaks when the file moves; parameterize the source.
Doing the final aggregation in 40 helper columns instead of Group By — rebuilding formula hell inside Power Query's output.
lessons.try_it: Rebuild one monthly formula-chain report as a Power Query: load, explicit types, merge, group. Time next month's refresh vs the old rebuild.

lessons.title: Auditing a Model Before It Ships
concepts: Audit with dollar impact: 'SUM misses the last row' becomes '$4,200 underpaid across 3 reps.' Impact converts a bug list into action — nobody prioritizes 'cell C47 is wrong.'

The structural audit checks: range boundaries (do SUMs cover new rows? Tables auto-expand), hardcoded constants (extract to an Assumptions sheet — every buried number is an unauditable decision), lookup exactness (approximate VLOOKUPs), and precedent tracing (does the logic flow make business sense?).

Check cells are the immune system: row totals vs column totals, inputs tie to sources, reasonableness bounds (commission between 0 and 50%?). A model without check cells is unauditable by construction.
The pre-decision gate: no model drives payouts, forecasts, or board numbers until the audit checklist is signed. 'We'll audit after' means the wrong number already shipped.

example.code:
Audit checklist (run before any decision use):
[ ] All constants on Assumptions sheet, named ranges
[ ] Ranges are Tables (auto-expand) or verified boundaries
[ ] Lookups exact-match (FALSE / XLOOKUP)
[ ] Check cells: totals tie, bounds sane, sources referenced
[ ] Spot-check 3 cases end-to-end, hand-calc vs model
[ ] Version + date stamped; change log started
example.walkthrough: Run the checklist top to bottom: extract constants first (the fastest way to find buried assumptions), verify ranges cover current data, flip lookups to exact match, then hand-calculate three cases end to end — the spot-check catches logic errors no structural check finds. Stamp the version; the audit is void the moment someone edits without logging.

pitfalls: Auditing without quantifying impact — the findings get deprioritized.
Fixing quietly without the checklist — the next model has the same diseases.
Spot-checking only the happy path; errors hide in edge cases (new reps, refunds, mid-period changes).
lessons.try_it: Audit a real workbook you depend on with this checklist; write up the top 3 findings with dollar impact and structural fixes.

lessons.title: Designing a Sound Test
concepts: Power analysis comes first: baseline rate, minimum detectable effect (MDE), significance level, and power determine the required sample size — and therefore the calendar duration. A test that can't reach its sample size can't answer its question.

Pre-register five things before launch: primary metric, MDE, sample size/duration, guardrail metrics with halt thresholds, and the ship/no-ship decision rule. Pre-registration is what separates experiments from fishing trips.
Choose the MDE from business relevance, not statistics: the smallest lift worth shipping. Detecting a 1% lift nobody would act on wastes weeks; the MDE should reflect the decision threshold.

Randomization unit must match the analysis unit and the user experience: user-level for user-facing changes (avoiding the same user seeing both variants), and stable cross-platform identity when users cross devices.

example.code:
Pre-registration doc:
  Primary metric: checkout conversion (visitor-level)
  Baseline: 5% | MDE: 10% relative (5% -> 5.5%) | alpha 0.05, power 80%
  Sample: ~60K visitors/arm -> ~12 days at 10K/day
  Guardrails: page load p95 (+200ms halt), support tickets (+10% halt)
  Decision: ship if primary significant AND guardrails clean
example.walkthrough: Start from the business question and pick the MDE worth acting on. Run the power math to get the sample size, convert to calendar days at your traffic, and sanity-check the timeline BEFORE promising results. Write the guardrails and decision rule down — the discipline of pre-registration is what makes the result trustworthy when it's inconvenient.

pitfalls: Launching without power analysis — the test is decorative, incapable of detecting the effect size that matters.
Letting the MDE be set by 'what we can detect in a week' instead of 'what's worth shipping.'
No guardrails on monetization or latency tests — the primary metric wins while the business loses.
lessons.try_it: Write a full pre-registration doc for a test you're considering: run the power math, convert to calendar days, and check whether the timeline is honest.

lessons.title: Reading Results Without Fooling Yourself
concepts: Check validity BEFORE the result: SRM check (sample ratio mismatch — did randomization actually split 50/50?), pre-period balance, and instrumentation (did the variant actually render?). Invalid tests produce confident wrong answers.

Peeking inflates false positives: each interim look is another chance to catch noise. Either hold the pre-registered duration or use sequential methods designed for peeking — chosen upfront, not retrofitted.

Read the confidence interval, not just the p-value: the CI shows the range of compatible effects. A 'significant' +0.1% with CI [0.01%, 0.2%] is a win nobody should ship; a null with CI [-5%, +5%] is 'couldn't tell,' not 'no effect.'

Post-hoc segments are hypothesis-generating: with 10 slices, ~40% chance of a false 'significant' segment. The valid question is the interaction test; surprising segments get replicated as new pre-registered tests, not shipped.

example.code:
Results checklist:
[ ] SRM check passed (50/50 split held)
[ ] Full pre-registered duration completed (no early stop)
[ ] CI read: effect range, not just p<0.05
[ ] Guardrails clean
[ ] Segments: interaction test or replicate, never ship post-hoc
Verdict options: SHIP / NO-SHIP / INCONCLUSIVE (rerun powered) / REPLICATE segment
example.walkthrough: Run validity checks first — an SRM failure voids everything below it. Confirm the duration was honored. Read the CI for the effect range and ask 'would we ship the bottom of this interval?' Check guardrails before celebrating. Treat segments as leads for the next test, not conclusions from this one. Four verdicts exist; 'ship because p<0.05' isn't one of them.

pitfalls: Reading the p-value without the CI — significance without magnitude is noise with confidence.
Shipping a post-hoc winning segment without replication.
Calling an underpowered null 'no effect' instead of 'inconclusive.'
lessons.try_it: Take a past test result and re-read it with this checklist: run the SRM math, read the CI's lower bound, and check whether the original verdict survives.

lessons.title: Designing DQ Monitors That Get Trusted
concepts: Layer the checks: hard invariants (no null primary keys, row counts reconcile source→mart, no future timestamps) page immediately — they can never be legitimate. Statistical checks (volume drift vs seasonal baseline) page on sustained deviation. Everything else goes to a daily digest.

Alert fatigue is the #1 monitor killer: a threshold that pages on every marketing campaign teaches the on-call to ignore pages, and the real incident pages into the void. Tune thresholds on historical data and MEASURE the false-positive rate before enabling pages.

Make alerts actionable: every page names the check, the expected vs observed value, the likely blast radius, and the first diagnostic step. 'Conversion rate anomaly' is noise; 'orders_mart row count 40% below 7-day median, check the API validation rejects' is a page worth waking for.
Cover the silent failures: validation rejections, dedup windows, late data — the failures that never error. Stage-to-stage count reconciliation is the instrument that makes silent drops visible.

example.code:
-- reconciliation check: counts at every handoff, daily
SELECT 'api' AS stage, COUNT(*) FROM raw_events WHERE dt = CURRENT_DATE
UNION ALL SELECT 'validated', COUNT(*) FROM validated_events WHERE dt = CURRENT_DATE
UNION ALL SELECT 'mart', COUNT(*) FROM orders_mart WHERE dt = CURRENT_DATE;
-- alert if any stage-to-stage drop exceeds 2x historical stddev
example.walkthrough: Instrument counts at every pipeline handoff — the reconciliation query above is the foundation. Set invariant alerts (null keys, count mismatches) to page, statistical alerts (drift vs baseline) to page on sustained deviation, and route the rest to a digest. Before go-live, backtest thresholds on 30 days of history and count the false pages; tune until the on-call trusts every page.

pitfalls: Flat thresholds on seasonal metrics — every campaign becomes a page, then pages become wallpaper.
Alerting on the metric without the diagnostic context — the on-call starts from zero at 3 AM.
Monitoring only failures, never silent drops — the pipeline is 'green' while eating 2% of rows weekly.
lessons.try_it: Design the three-layer monitor set for one pipeline you own: 3 invariants, 2 statistical checks, and the digest list. Backtest the statistical thresholds on last month's data.

lessons.title: Root-Causing Data Incidents
concepts: Follow the evidence chain, not the org chart: symptom → stage-to-stage counts → the handoff where rows vanish or corrupt → deploy timelines and validation rule diffs around that time. The culprit is usually a change, and changes have timestamps.

Correlate ruthlessly: the duplicate spike started Tuesday; what deployed Tuesday? The null surge matches a schema change; diff the schemas. Incident timelines are built from logs and deploys, not opinions.

Distinguish the failure classes: outage (loud, cliff-shaped), silent drop (validation/dedup eating rows steadily), semantic break (schema/type change corrupting meaning), and upstream change (source behavior shifted). Each class has a different fix location.

The incident isn't over at recovery: the postmortem must produce the structural prevention (the reconciliation check, the contract, the CI validation) — otherwise you've scheduled the next incident, not prevented it.

example.code:
Incident timeline template:
  T-0: symptom detected (orders -30%, alert fired)
  T+10m: stage counts -> drop between validated and mart
  T+20m: deploy log -> mobile team shipped schema v14 at T-2h
  T+30m: schema diff -> 'email' field renamed to 'email_address'
  T+40m: validation rule drops rows missing 'email'
  Root cause: uncontracted schema rename. Fix + contract + CI check.
example.walkthrough: Build the timeline as you investigate: symptom time, then walk the stage counts to find the losing handoff, then pull deploy logs and schema diffs around that window. Name the failure class — here, an uncontracted schema change causing silent validation drops. Fix the data, then fix the system: the contract and CI check are the real deliverables of the incident.

pitfalls: Stopping at recovery ('data's back') without the structural prevention — guaranteeing recurrence.
Blaming the pipeline when the source changed — fix location follows the evidence, not the team boundary.
Postmortems that document what happened but assign no prevention owner and date.
lessons.try_it: Write a postmortem for a past data incident using the timeline template; end with the structural prevention item, an owner, and a date.

Confounders — rule: always segment by known confounders (device, source, region) before trusting an aggregate — the overall number can lie while every segment tells the truth.
A/B testing — proper A/B: randomize, pre-register the primary metric and runtime, size for statistical power (enough users to detect a meaningful effect), then read significance at the end.
